words: push; pull; strong; gentle; direction; move; stop; roll
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare which push made the ball go farther)
notes: The first investigation of the year, so it also teaches the K-2 observing practice every later row uses: notice with the senses and a hand lens, say what you notice and wonder, record with a labelled drawing, a tally or a dot on a class chart. Then plan and carry out, with the class, a test of what a bigger or smaller push or pull does to how an object moves, and what pushing from a different direction does: a ball rolled with a gentle and a strong push, a box pulled by a string, a rolling ball stopped by a hand, two balls bumping. Students compare which went farther or faster in relative words. The reasoning that grows: a push or pull causes a change in motion, and a bigger push causes a bigger change (introduces cause-effect). Boundary: only strength or direction is varied in one test, never both at once; only contact pushes and pulls, no magnets. Teacher note: rolling and pulling stays on the floor in a cleared space; no throwing; no tasting or sniffing unknown things during observation. Vocabulary (K to 2): the words of this grade are taught as spoken and visual language, said aloud, shown with objects and labelled on pictures; students are not expected to decode them alone.

words: ramp; speed; faster; slower; turn; path; works; test
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare distances and speeds directly)
notes: A design problem: make a ball or marble roll a set distance, follow a path, turn a corner or knock down a target, using ramps, blocks, books and card walls. Students try a solution, watch whether it does what was wanted and use simple results (did it reach the line, yes or no; which ramp sent it farther) to decide whether the design works as intended. The reasoning that grows: a designed object changes speed or direction by pushing on the ball, and a test tells whether it works. Boundary: friction is not taught as the reason a ball slows. Uses the design steps from sk-define-problem. Teacher note: marbles are a choking hazard for some kindergarten children; use larger balls or close supervision.

words: sunlight; shade; warm; warmer; cool; cooler; surface
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare two surfaces: warmer or cooler)
notes: Observe that sunlight warms the Earth's surface: touch sand, soil, rocks and a pan of water in the sun and in the shade, morning and afternoon, and record which is warmer. The reasoning that grows: sunlight causes the warming, so the same thing in shade is cooler. Boundary: temperature only in relative words (warmer, cooler); no thermometer readings are required. Teacher note: dark surfaces such as pavement or metal can be hot enough to hurt; the teacher checks first and students touch with the back of a hand briefly; never look at the sun.

words: problem; solve; design; build; idea; tool
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.3 (ask questions to get information about the problem)
notes: Owns K-2-ETS1-1, done in full here: before building, students ask questions, observe and gather information about a situation people want to change, and say the problem in one sentence ("The slide is too hot to use after lunch"; "The ball will not reach the bin"). Introduces the design-cycle as three steps a kindergartner can say: what is the problem, try an idea, test it. Practised through the kindergarten design problems (sk-ramp-design, sk-shade-design, sk-reduce-impact) rather than as a separate unit. Grade 1 adds a sketch of how shape helps function (s1-sketch-shape); grade 2 adds comparing two designs by test data (s2-compare-designs). Later grades redefine the problem with criteria and constraints (grades 3 to 5).

words: shade; structure; block; cover; umbrella; tent
cross_subject: math:K.MD.A.2 (compare the spot under the shade with a spot in the sun)
notes: Use tools and materials to design and build a structure that reduces the warming effect of sunlight on a small area (a shade for a toy animal, a sandbox corner or an ice cube), then test it by comparing the shaded spot with one in the sun. The reasoning that grows: blocking sunlight causes less warming, so the material and shape of the cover matter. Uses sk-sun-warms and the design steps of sk-define-problem. Boundary: relative warmer or cooler only. Teacher note: scissors are child-safe; check surfaces before touching as in sk-sun-warms.

words: living; need; food; water; air; light; plant; animal; survive
cross_subject: math:K.MD.B.3 (sort living things into groups and count each group)
notes: Use observations of class plants, a class animal or schoolyard life, pictures and video to describe patterns in what plants and animals, people included, need to survive: all need water; animals take in food and plants do not; different animals eat different foods (some eat plants, some eat other animals); plants need light. Introduces the patterns model: the same thing seen again and again across many living things. Boundary: no photosynthesis, no food chains; plants making their own food is grade 5. Handoff to s2-plant-needs-test skips grade 1 because grade 1 has no plant-needs expectation; grade 2 tests the need for light and water by experiment. Teacher note: class animals are cared for humanely and handled only with an adult; check food and pet allergies before any animal or animal food comes into the room.

words: weather; sunny; cloudy; rainy; windy; warm; cool; chart; pattern
cross_subject: math:K.MD.B.3 (count sunny, cloudy and rainy days and sort the counts)
notes: Observe and record local weather each day on a class chart (sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy; warmer or cooler), then share and read the chart for patterns over time: it is usually cooler in the morning than the afternoon; one month had more sunny days than another. Introduces data-graph as a class picture graph or tally chart, and patterns over time, using the observing and recording habits begun in sk-push-pull. Boundary: counts are whole numbers and temperature is relative (warmer, cooler). Keep the chart all year so grade 1 sky and daylight work can lean on the habit.

words: forecast; storm; severe; warning; prepare; safe
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.3 (ask and answer questions to get information)
notes: Ask questions to find out why people forecast the weather: a forecast tells us severe weather may be coming so we can get ready and stay safe. Students ask a visiting adult, watch a short forecast and look at a picture book to answer their own questions, then name what the school and families do for the local kinds of severe weather (storm, blizzard, heat, flood, tornado or hurricane as fits the region). The reasoning: knowing what is coming causes people to prepare. The obtaining-information practice passes to grade 1 (reading texts and media, s1-parent-offspring); the Earth-events thread passes to grade 2 (s2-fast-slow-events), skipping grade 1 because grade 1 has no Earth-events expectation. Teacher note: severe weather can frighten young children and some have lived through a disaster; keep the focus on safety plans and helpers, and do not ask children to retell frightening events.

words: change; environment; dig; build; claim; evidence; because
cross_subject: ela:W.K.1 (draw and tell an opinion with a reason)
notes: Make a claim and back it with evidence: plants and animals, people included, change their surroundings to get what they need. Evidence from photographs, video and the schoolyard: a squirrel digs to hide food, tree roots crack a sidewalk, beavers build a dam, birds build nests, people clear land for houses. Introduces claim-evidence-reasoning at its simplest: I think ..., because I saw ... Students draw and tell, with the teacher writing. Builds on the needs patterns of sk-living-needs.

words: live; home; place; meadow; forest; pond; together; system
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.5 (add drawings to a description)
notes: Use a model (a drawing, a class diorama or a picture map) to show how what a plant or animal needs connects to where it lives: deer eat buds and leaves so they live near forests; grass needs sunlight so it grows in open meadows; fish need water so they live in ponds. Plants, animals and their surroundings together are a system (introduces system-model as parts that need each other). Uses the needs patterns of sk-living-needs. Handoff to s2-habitat-diversity skips grade 1 because grade 1 has no habitat expectation; grade 1 carries the system-model through the parts of organisms (s1-parts-mimic).

words: reuse; recycle; reduce; waste; protect; land; water; air
cross_subject: ela:W.K.2 (draw, tell and write to inform others)
notes: Communicate solutions that lessen people's effect on the local land, water, air and living things: cutting trees to make paper, using materials to make bottles, litter in the schoolyard; solutions such as reusing paper, recycling cans and bottles, a class litter pick-up. Students choose one solution, explain in drawing and words why it helps, and share it with another class or families (a poster or short talk). Uses the design steps of sk-define-problem and the cause-effect thinking of sk-sun-warms. No in-band handoff: the thread picks up in grades 3 to 5 (human impact and solutions). Teacher note: litter pick-ups use gloves and grabbers, no glass or sharp items, adults bag the waste.

words: sound; vibrate; vibration; pluck; loud; soft; tuning fork
cross_subject: ela:W.1.8 (recall information from the investigation to answer a question)
notes: Plan and carry out, with peers and teacher guidance, investigations that give evidence that vibrating materials make sound and that sound can make materials vibrate: pluck a stretched rubber band, tap a drum with rice on top, touch a humming throat, hold paper near a speaker, a tuning fork touched to water. The reasoning that grows from kindergarten: a push or pluck (sk-push-pull) sets the material moving back and forth, and that motion causes the sound. Planning grows from the class tests of sk-push-pull: students now say what they will do and what they will watch for. Boundary: no wave model, wavelength or speed of sound; waves are grade 4. Teacher note: keep sounds at classroom level and never near ears; rubber bands are held so they cannot snap toward faces; eye protection if anything can fly. Vocabulary (K to 2): the words of this grade are taught as spoken and visual language, said aloud, shown with objects and labelled on pictures; students are not expected to decode them alone.

words: light; dark; see; light source; shine; illuminate
cross_subject: ela:W.1.2 (write an explanation with facts)
notes: Make observations (a dark box with a peephole, a darkened room, a video of a cave explorer with a flashlight) to build an evidence-based account that we see objects only when light shines on them, from a light source such as the sun, a lamp or a flashlight, or when the object gives off its own light. The sun from sk-sun-warms is now named as a light source. The account uses claim-evidence-reasoning from sk-change-environment, now written with a sentence frame. Boundary: no light entering the eye or reflection model; that is grade 4. Teacher note: never look at the sun or shine a light into anyone's eyes; some children fear the dark, so let them hold the flashlight or sit by the door.

words: transparent; translucent; opaque; reflect; mirror; beam; shadow
cross_subject: math:1.MD.C.4 (sort the materials into three groups and count each)
notes: Plan and carry out an investigation of what happens when objects of different materials are put in a beam of light: clear plastic lets light through (transparent), wax paper lets some through (translucent), cardboard blocks it and makes a shadow (opaque), a mirror sends it a new way (reflective). The reasoning that grows from sk-shade-design: the material, not just the shape, decides how much light gets through. Planning grows from sk-push-pull: students choose the materials and keep the flashlight in the same place. Boundary: no speed of light. Teacher note: mirrors are plastic or edge-taped; no lasers.

words: signal; message; send; receive; distance; device; code
cross_subject: math:1.MD.A.2 (measure how far the signal reached in length units)
notes: Use tools and materials to design and build a device that uses light or sound to send a message across a distance: a cup-and-string telephone, a flashlight blink code, a pattern of drum beats. Students define the problem (sk-define-problem), build, then test whether the message got through at a longer distance, as in sk-ramp-design they judge whether the design works as intended. Uses the sound and light ideas of this year. Strand engineering because the expectation is a design task. Boundary: no technical details of how phones or radios work. Teacher note: string under tension at face height is a trip and eye hazard; flashlights are never pointed at eyes.

hands_on: s2-habitat-diversity; s2-seed-pollinator-model; s3-variation-advantage; s4-structures-function; s4-senses-brain; s2-plant-needs-test
words: root; stem; leaf; flower; fruit; shell; claw; part; job; mimic; protect
cross_subject: ela:RI.1.2 (find the main topic and key details in an informational text)
notes: Two moves in one expectation. First the core idea: plants and animals have outside parts that help them survive, grow and meet their needs (roots take in water and hold the plant, leaves face the light, a turtle's shell protects it, a hawk's eyes find food), and animals sense and respond to what is around them. Students observe real plants, pictures and video and record part and job in a two-column chart. This builds on sk-living-needs (what living things need) and sk-needs-places (the system-model): each living thing is itself made of parts that work together. Introduces structure-function: the shape of a part fits its job. Then the design that completes 1-LS1-1: use materials to solve a human problem by copying how a plant or animal uses its parts (a helmet like a turtle shell or acorn cap, a stand that will not tip like roots or a tail, a fence with spikes like thorns, an alarm that hears like big ears). Students define the human problem (sk-define-problem) and build; the planned sketch is the work of s1-sketch-shape. Teacher note: no handling of wild animals; plant parts are not tasted. Retrieves the plant needs of sk-living-needs (roots take in water, leaves face the light) and hands them to s2-plant-needs-test, which tests them.

words: sketch; drawing; label; model; shape; plan
cross_subject: ela:SL.1.5 (add drawings to make an idea clear)
notes: Owns K-2-ETS1-2, done in full here: develop a simple sketch, labelled drawing or physical model to show how the shape of an object helps it work to solve a given problem, and use it to explain the design to others. Practised through s1-parts-mimic (shape copied from nature) and s1-signal-device (cup shape, string length). In kindergarten students built and showed (sk-ramp-design, sk-shade-design) without a planned sketch; grade 2 tests two such designs against each other with data (s2-compare-designs). The design-cycle grows a step: problem, sketch, build, test.

words: parent; offspring; young; protect; feed; signal; cry
cross_subject: ela:RI.1.1 (ask and answer questions about key details in a text)
notes: Read texts and use media (picture books, short video) to find patterns in how parents and young behave to help the young survive: the young signal (crying, cheeping, calling) and parents respond (feeding, comforting, carrying, protecting). The obtaining-information practice grows from sk-forecast-severe: now students read and compare more than one source for the same pattern. Teacher note: families differ (one parent, grandparents, foster and adoptive families); keep examples to animals and never ask a child to describe their own family. Also hands on to s7-interaction-patterns, where behaviour patterns return as interactions between populations.

words: alike; different; young; parent; same kind; trait
cross_subject: math:1.MD.A.1 (order leaves by length)
notes: Make observations to build an evidence-based account that young plants and animals are like, but not exactly like, their parents: leaves from one kind of plant share a shape but differ in size; puppies look like their parents but not exactly. Students line up leaves by length and compare photographs of animal families. claim-evidence-reasoning grows from sk-change-environment: the claim now rests on measured or listed differences. Boundary: no inheritance or genes, no animals that change form (metamorphosis), no hybrids. Teacher note: do not ask children to compare themselves with their parents (adoption, foster care, family separation); use plants and animals.

words: sun; moon; star; rise; set; sky; day; night
cross_subject: ela:W.1.8 (recall observations to answer a question)
notes: Use observations of the sun, moon and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted: the sun and moon seem to rise on one side of the sky, move across it and set; stars other than the sun are seen at night and not in the day. Students mark the sun's place from one window or a shadow stick at three times of day and keep a moon drawing log at home and school, extending the daily record habit of sk-weather-watch. Boundary: star patterns only as seen at night, not in the day; no Earth turning or orbit model (that is grade 5). Teacher note: never look straight at the sun; observe its position by shadows.

words: daylight; season; winter; spring; summer; fall; longer; shorter
cross_subject: math:1.MD.C.4 (organise and compare data in up to three groups)
notes: Make observations at different times of year to relate the amount of daylight to the season: is it dark or light at the same clock time (going-home time) in fall, winter and spring? The class records it on a chart and compares, finding that winter has less daylight than spring or fall. data-graph grows from the kindergarten weather chart: now a chart the class reads to compare categories. Boundary: relative amounts only, no counting hours of daylight. Needs a record kept across the year, so the unit opens in fall and closes in spring.

words: material; property; hard; soft; bendy; rough; smooth; sort
cross_subject: ela:W.2.7 (record science observations in a shared project)
notes: Plan and carry out an investigation to describe and sort different materials (wood, metal, plastic, fabric, paper, rubber, glass shown not handled) by properties they can observe: colour, texture, hardness, flexibility, and whether light passes through (from s1-light-materials). Patterns: different objects can share a property; one material can be found in many objects. Students design the sorting tests (scratch, bend, press). Boundary: observable properties only, no measured mass or volume (grade 5). Teacher note: no glass or sharp metal in student hands. Vocabulary (K to 2): the words of this grade are taught as spoken and visual language, said aloud, shown with objects and labelled on pictures; students are not expected to decode them alone.

words: strong; absorb; flexible; test; best; purpose; data
cross_subject: math:2.MD.D.10 (draw a bar graph of the test results)
notes: Analyse data from testing materials to decide which has the properties that best suit a purpose: which paper towel soaks up most water, which fabric is best for a raincoat, which material makes the strongest bridge deck. Students run the tests, measure in length where they measure (how far the water climbed, how far the deck bent), make a bar graph and argue for a choice. data-graph grows from s1-daylight-seasons to a bar graph students draw; structure-function grows from s1-sketch-shape: material as well as shape fits the job. Boundary: quantitative measures are length only. Teacher note: wipe up water at once. Hands on to s5-identify-materials, where measured and observed properties identify a material.

words: piece; part; whole; take apart; build; new
cross_subject: ela:W.2.8 (recall information from experience to answer a question)
notes: Make observations to build an evidence-based account of how an object made of a small set of pieces (blocks, building bricks, a set of shapes) can be taken apart and made into a new object: the same pieces, a different whole. The evidence-based account grows from s1-see-with-light. The system-model returns as parts and whole. This is the first step toward the grade 5 idea that matter is made of pieces too small to see and is not lost when things change; no particle model is introduced here.

words: heat; cool; melt; freeze; change; reverse; change back
cross_subject: ela:W.2.1 (write an opinion with reasons)
notes: Make an argument from evidence that some changes caused by heating or cooling can be reversed and some cannot: water freezes and melts back, butter or chocolate melts and hardens again; an egg once cooked, a leaf once frozen and thawed, paper once heated stay changed. The argument grows from s1-like-parents: a claim, evidence from observation and a reason. Boundary: no particle explanation (grade 5). Teacher note: all heating is done by an adult with a warm-water bath or hot plate kept out of reach, never a flame near students; check egg, dairy and other food allergies; nothing is eaten. Practice link: s1-like-parents is assumed for the claim-evidence-reasoning practice, not for its content.

words: grow; sunlight; water; test; fair; change one thing; measure
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure plant height with a ruler)
notes: Plan and carry out an investigation to find out whether plants need sunlight and water to grow: one set of seedlings with light and water, one in the dark, one without water, everything else kept the same. Students measure height and draw how the plants look over two to three weeks and graph the results. Tests the kindergarten claim (sk-living-needs) by experiment; that handoff skips grade 1 because grade 1 has no plant-needs expectation. Planning grows from s1-light-materials to a fair test. Boundary: one variable at a time. Teacher note: discard mouldy soil promptly; wash hands after handling soil. Also assumes s1-parts-mimic (grade 1: roots take in water and leaves face the light), which keeps the kindergarten plant needs in use. Handoff kind: from sk-living-needs (kindergarten) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s1-parts-mimic.

words: seed; spread; pollen; pollinate; flower; depend
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure how far a model seed travels)
notes: Develop a simple model that copies what an animal does to spread seeds or carry pollen: a sock or fuzzy glove walked through a field of burr-like seeds, a pipe-cleaner "bee" that moves pollen (chalk dust or powdered drink mix) from flower to flower. The model shows a plant and an animal depending on each other (system-model). It reverses the design of s1-parts-mimic: there people copied nature; here a model copies the animal's job. Teacher note: no live bees; check pollen and dust allergies; burrs kept away from hair and eyes.

words: habitat; land; water; many kinds; diversity; survey; compare
cross_subject: math:2.MD.D.10 (picture graph of how many kinds were found in each place)
notes: Make observations of plants and animals to compare how many different kinds live in different habitats: a schoolyard survey of two spots (lawn and garden bed, or sunny and shady), then photographs and video of a pond, a forest, a desert and an ocean shore. Students count kinds, not names, and graph them. Uses the parts-and-needs reasoning of s1-parts-mimic and the system-model of sk-needs-places (that handoff skips grade 1, which has no habitat expectation). Boundary: specific plant and animal names in specific habitats are not assessed. Teacher note: outdoor survey rules (no touching unknown plants or animals, stay in sight, return anything moved); check for stinging insects and allergies. Handoff kind: from sk-needs-places (kindergarten) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s1-parts-mimic.

words: land; water; hill; valley; mountain; river; lake; ocean; map
cross_subject: social-studies:ss1-landforms-waters (landforms and bodies of water named in grade 1)
notes: Develop a model (a sand-tray landscape, clay relief or picture map with a key) to show the shapes and kinds of land and bodies of water in an area: the local area first, then a contrasting one. Students find patterns (rivers run downhill to lakes or oceans). Boundary: no quantitative scaling in the model. The map key and landform words lean on social studies grade 1 and 2 map work; science adds the model as a thing to reason with. No in-band assumes: kindergarten and grade 1 science have no landform expectation.

words: ocean; river; lake; pond; ice; glacier; solid; liquid
cross_subject: ela:W.2.8 (gather information from provided sources to answer a question)
notes: Obtain information from texts, maps and video to find where water is found on Earth (oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds, ice and snow) and that it can be solid or liquid. Connects to the solid and liquid water of s2-heat-cool-change. The obtaining-information practice grows from s1-parent-offspring: now students record facts from two sources on one chart. Boundary: no water cycle (grade 5 and middle school) and no amounts. Practice link: s1-parent-offspring is assumed for the obtaining-information practice (reading more than one source), not for its content.

words: quick; slow; earthquake; volcano; erosion; landslide; change; time
cross_subject: ela:RI.2.3 (describe how events in a text connect)
notes: Use information from several sources (photographs, video, simple texts) to give evidence that some Earth events happen quickly (a volcano erupting, an earthquake, a landslide, a flood) and others slowly (a canyon carved by a river, a rock worn smooth). Introduces stability-change (a model name added by this band for the stability and change crosscutting concept, which no shared name covers): the land looks the same day to day but changes, fast or slow. Builds on sk-forecast-severe (severe weather as an event people prepare for; skips grade 1, which has no Earth-events expectation) and on the reading of sources in s1-parent-offspring. Boundary: no measured time scales. Teacher note: disaster images can upset children who have lived through one; choose images without injured people and stress helpers and safety. Handoff kind: from sk-forecast-severe (kindergarten) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s1-parent-offspring.

words: erosion; wind; water; wall; windbreak; roots; protect
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure how much sand washed away in centimetres)
notes: Compare several solutions designed to slow or stop wind or water from changing the shape of the land: in a tray of sand and soil, walls, rock barriers, grass mats and stick windbreaks are tested against poured water or a fan, and the class measures how far the land wore back. Uses stability-change from s2-fast-slow-events and the design-cycle from s1-signal-device; the comparison of two tested designs is the work of s2-compare-designs. Teacher note: fans run only on low with fingers clear; water spills are wiped at once to stop slips; wash hands after soil.

words: compare; better; worse; strength; weakness; test; data
cross_subject: math:2.MD.D.10 (bar graph to compare two designs)
notes: Owns K-2-ETS1-3, done in full here: analyse data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem and say what each does well and poorly. Practised through s2-erosion-solutions (two barrier designs) and s2-best-material (two materials). Grows from kindergarten, where students only judged whether one design worked (sk-ramp-design), and grade 1, where they sketched and explained one design (s1-sketch-shape). The full K-2 design-cycle is now: define the problem, sketch, build, test, compare. Grades 3 to 5 add criteria, constraints and fair tests of many solutions.

words: force; push; pull; balanced; unbalanced; direction; gravity; motion; fair test; variable
notes: Plan and run, as a class at first and then in small groups, a fair test of what a push or pull does to an object's motion: change one thing at a time (how many pushes, how strong compared with another, which direction) and keep the rest the same. Balanced forces (equal pushes from both sides on a box) give no change in motion; an unbalanced force starts, stops, speeds up or turns an object. Introduces the force arrow drawing (an arrow shows the direction of a push or pull, a longer arrow a stronger one) as a model students revise. Gravity is named as a pull toward the ground. Boundary: one variable at a time; force size is compared, never measured in units; gravity only as a pull down. First fair test of the band (Appendix F, 3-5 investigations). Skips grade 4 to s5-gravity-down because grade 4 has no forces standard; grade 4's s4-collisions carries the force arrow so the model has no gap. Across bands it assumes sk-push-pull (kindergarten: pushes and pulls change motion, a stronger push a bigger change; skips because grades 1 and 2 have no forces standard). Handoff kind: from sk-push-pull (kindergarten) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: motion; pattern; predict; observe; measure; record; swing; back and forth
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.4 (measuring lengths to the half and quarter inch for how far an object moves)
notes: Observe and measure motion that repeats (a swing, a ball rolling back and forth in a bowl, a see-saw, a pendulum of string and washers) and record it in a table so the pattern shows; use the pattern to predict where the object will be next and test the prediction. The reasoning that grows: a pattern in the data lets you predict, and a prediction that fails tells you something changed. Boundary: no technical words such as period or frequency. Hands on to s4-speed-energy the habit of describing motion by how fast and how far. Across bands it assumes s1-sky-patterns (grade 1: predicting a motion from its observed pattern (sun and moon); skips because grade 2 has no motion standard). Practice link: s1-sky-patterns is assumed for the patterns practice (predicting a motion from its observed pattern), not for its content. Handoff kind: from s1-sky-patterns (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: magnet; attract; repel; pole; static electricity; charge; distance; non-contact force
cross_subject: ela:SL.3.1 (asking and answering questions in a collaborative discussion)
notes: Ask testable questions about pushes and pulls between objects that do not touch, then investigate them: magnet to magnet, magnet to steel paper clips, one magnet against two, a charged balloon and hair or bits of paper. Cause and effect to find: closer objects push or pull more strongly, and turning a magnet around changes attract to repel. Force arrows are drawn between objects that are not touching. Boundary: only objects students can handle; electric effects only as static electricity (no circuits here). Teacher note: small and strong magnets are a swallowing hazard for young children and harm devices and cards; count magnets out and back. Skips grade 4 to s5-gravity-down (gravity also pulls without touching), since grade 4 teaches no forces standard. Across bands it assumes sk-push-pull (kindergarten: pushes and pulls as causes of motion; skips because grades 1 and 2 have no forces standard). Also hands on to s8-potential-energy. Handoff kind: from sk-push-pull (kindergarten) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: design problem; need; want; criteria; constraint; materials; cost; time; solution
cross_subject: math:3.MD.A.2 (measuring masses in grams when a criterion is how much the latch must hold)
notes: Define a simple design problem that magnets can solve (a latch that keeps a cupboard door shut, a way to keep two moving toy cars from touching), written as the need, the criteria for success and the constraints on materials, time and cost. The band's engineering standard 3-5-ETS1-1 is done in full here: students state the problem precisely enough that two solutions could be judged against it. They may sketch and try one solution, but comparing many solutions is grade 4 (s4-information-codes, 3-5-ETS1-2) and fair tests of a prototype are grade 5 (s5-design-test, 3-5-ETS1-3). Grade 3's other design work, judging the merit of solutions in s3-environment-change-solution and s3-weather-hazard, uses the criteria language set here. Teacher note: the magnet swallowing and device warnings of s3-magnet-static apply. Across bands it assumes s2-compare-designs (grade 2: stating a problem and judging designs against it).

words: life cycle; birth; growth; reproduction; death; seed; egg; larva; adult; flowering plant
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.7 (using diagrams and illustrations to understand a text)
notes: Develop models (drawn cycles, sequenced cards, a class chart) of life cycles of several organisms, watched where possible (bean or radish plants, mealworms or butterflies), and compare them: every cycle differs in its stages and timing, yet all share birth, growth, reproduction and death. The changes form a pattern. Students revise the model when observation shows a stage they missed. Boundary: plant life cycles are flowering plants only; human reproduction is not included. Teacher note: care for living things humanely and return or release them as local rules allow; check allergies before handling plants, soil or insects. Across bands it assumes s2-seed-pollinator-model (grade 2: plants depend on animals to move pollen and seeds, steps in a flowering plant life).

words: group; herd; flock; pack; colony; survive; protect; claim; evidence; reason
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (writing an opinion with reasons that support it)
notes: Construct an argument, with a claim, evidence and reasoning, that some animals form groups that help their members survive: wolves hunt in packs, fish school, bees divide work, musk oxen circle against predators. Evidence comes from video, data on hunting success or survival in groups and alone, and readings. The reasoning that grows: the claim is about cause (being in a group makes survival more likely), and some animals live alone and survive in other ways, which a good argument admits. Social interactions only at the level of what the group does, no animal behavior mechanisms. Across bands it assumes s1-parent-offspring (grade 1: animal behaviours that help the young survive; skips because grade 2 has no animal behaviour standard). Handoff kind: from s1-parent-offspring (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: trait; inherit; parent; offspring; sibling; variation; similar; different
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.3 (scaled bar graphs to compare how many offspring show each trait)
notes: Analyze and interpret data (photos, tallies, bar graphs) to show that young plants and animals have traits like their parents and that individuals of the same kind still vary: puppies in a litter, kittens, seedlings from one packet, ear length in rabbits. Patterns to find are the likenesses between parents and offspring and the differences among siblings. Boundary: no genes or other mechanism of inheritance, no predicting traits, and non-human examples only (so no student is asked about family resemblance). Sets up s3-environment-traits, which separates inherited traits from traits the environment shapes. Across bands it assumes s1-like-parents (grade 1: young are like but not exactly like their parents; skips because grade 2 has no heredity standard). Handoff kind: from s1-like-parents (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: environment; influence; inherited; grown; stunted; evidence; explanation
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.4 (measuring plant heights in inches and halves of inches)
notes: Use evidence to support the explanation that the environment can change a trait: the same kind of plant grown with too little water or light is shorter and paler; a dog fed too much and walked too little gets heavy; flamingos fed less shrimp turn paler. A class plant investigation (same seeds, one condition changed) gives first-hand evidence. Comes after s3-inherited-traits in the year so students can sort traits into inherited, shaped by the environment, or both. Teacher note: do not use people's weight or bodies as examples. Skips grade 4 to s5-plant-matter: grade 4 has no plant growth standard, and grade 5 reuses this plant-growth investigation to ask where the plant's matter comes from. Across bands it assumes s2-plant-needs-test (grade 2: a fair test showing plants short of water or light grow poorly).

words: fossil; extinct; environment; long ago; ancient; layer; marine; relative age
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.7 (reading information from pictures, maps and charts of fossil finds)
notes: Analyze and interpret data from fossils (kind, size and where they are found) as evidence of the organisms that lived long ago and the environments they lived in: sea shells on dry land show sea once covered it, tropical plant fossils in the Arctic show a once-warm climate, and fossils of extinct organisms show living things have changed. Older fossils lie deeper in undisturbed layers, so ages are relative. Boundary: no naming of specific fossils or modern species to memorize; major fossil types and relative age only. BASELINE rule 5: Earth's long history is stated as the evidence shows. Hands on to s4-rock-layers, which uses fossils in rock layers to explain how a landscape changed. Across bands it assumes s2-fast-slow-events (grade 2: Earth events over very long times). Also hands on to s8-anatomical-relationships.

words: variation; advantage; survive; camouflage; predator; prey; mate; offspring; characteristic
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.3 (describing cause and effect relationships in a science text)
notes: Use evidence to build an explanation for how differences among individuals of one kind give some of them an advantage in surviving, finding mates and having young: plants with larger thorns are eaten less, better-camouflaged moths are found by birds less often (a camouflage hunt with colored paper on a patterned background gives class data). The reasoning that grows: a small difference, through cause and effect, changes who survives and leaves offspring. Structure and function returns from K-2 (thorns, coloring). No natural selection by name and no genetics; that is grade 8 (MS-LS4-4). Across bands it assumes s1-parts-mimic (grade 1: body parts that help plants and animals survive; skips because grade 2 has no structure standard). Also hands on to s8-selection-math. Handoff kind: from s1-parts-mimic (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: habitat; survive; need; ecosystem; system; depend; adapted; food; shelter
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (an opinion piece with reasons, here a claim about a habitat)
notes: Construct an argument with evidence that in a given habitat some organisms survive well, some less well and some not at all, using the organisms' needs and characteristics and the habitat's conditions (a cactus in a desert and in a bog, a polar bear and a frog in the Arctic). The organisms and their habitat form a system whose parts depend on each other, so the system model from K-2 grows here. Skips grade 4 to s5-matter-movement: grade 4 has no ecosystem standard, and grade 5's model of matter moving in an ecosystem builds on this habitat-as-system idea. Across bands it assumes s2-habitat-diversity (grade 2: different habitats hold different kinds of living things). Also hands on to s8-selection-math.

words: environmental change; habitat; solution; merit; criteria; migrate; problem
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.8 (connecting sentences and paragraphs in a text to see cause and effect)
notes: Make a claim about the merit of a solution to a problem caused when an environment changes and the plants and animals there change too: wildlife crossings over a new highway, a fish ladder at a dam, replanting after a fire. Students judge each solution against criteria stated the way s3-design-problem taught. Boundary: a single environmental change at a time; the greenhouse effect and climate change are not assessed here. BASELINE rule 5: if students raise climate change, answer it plainly as the evidence shows; it is taught in grades 6 to 8. Strand life because the core idea is LS4.D; the design reasoning is engineering practice. Across bands it assumes sk-reduce-impact (kindergarten: a solution that lessens harm to land and living things; skips because grades 1 and 2 have no human-impact standard). stability-change (from s2-fast-slow-events) carries here: an environment changes and some living things survive while others do not. Also hands on to s7-ecosystem-disruption, s7-population-consumption and s7-biodiversity-solutions, the grade 7 human impact and ecosystem rows. Handoff kind: from sk-reduce-impact (kindergarten) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: weather; season; temperature; precipitation; wind direction; average; table; bar graph; pictograph
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.3 (scaled picture graphs and bar graphs)
notes: Represent weather data in tables, pictographs and bar graphs to describe the weather typical of each season in a place: monthly average temperature, rainfall or snowfall, and wind direction, from the class's own weather log and from local records. Seasonal and monthly averages are supplied (from local records, or worked out by the teacher from the class log); students read, compare and graph them and do not calculate a mean, which math teaches in grade 6 (6.SP.B.5). The reasoning that grows: one day's weather is not a season's; typical conditions come from many days. Boundary: graphs limited to pictographs and bar graphs; climate change is not assessed. Paced after grade 3 math has taught scaled bar graphs (3.MD.B.3). Hands on to s4-weathering-erosion the habit of recording measurements in a table and graphing them. Across bands it assumes sk-weather-watch (kindergarten: a weather record read for patterns; skips because grades 1 and 2 have no weather standard). Handoff kind: from sk-weather-watch (kindergarten) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: climate; region; weather; equator; pole; tropical; desert; polar; temperate
cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-globe-grid (equator and poles on the globe, why places near the equator are warm); ela:RI.3.9 (comparing the key points of two texts on one topic)
notes: Obtain and combine information from texts, maps and data to describe the climates of different regions of the world, and tell climate (the pattern over many years) from weather (today). Patterns to find: warm near the equator and cold near the poles, wet and dry places. Comes after s3-weather-data in the year so typical conditions are already a known idea. No climate causes (the sun's angle, ocean currents) beyond the pattern. Skips grade 4 to s5-sphere-interactions, because grade 4 has no weather or climate standard and grade 5 explains how ocean and air shape climate. Across bands it assumes s2-land-water-model (grade 2: a model of the land and water of an area, read as a region).

words: hazard; flood; storm; lightning; barrier; levee; lightning rod; design solution; merit; reduce
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (opinion writing with reasons, here a claim about a design)
notes: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impact of a weather-related hazard (a flood barrier, a wind-resistant roof, a lightning rod), judged against criteria and constraints. Students may build and test a quick model (a roof that stays on under a fan) to give their claim evidence. Humans cannot stop severe weather but can lessen its harm. Teacher note: some students may have lived through floods, fires or storms; keep examples general and let students choose whether to share. Hands on to s4-hazard-solutions, which generates and compares several solutions for earthquakes, floods and volcanoes. Across bands it assumes sk-forecast-severe (kindergarten: forecasts help people prepare for severe weather; skips because grades 1 and 2 have no weather-hazard standard); s2-erosion-solutions (grade 2: comparing solutions that protect land from wind and water). Handoff kind: from sk-forecast-severe (kindergarten) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: energy; speed; faster; slower; motion energy; evidence; explanation
cross_subject: ela:W.4.2 (an informative text that explains with facts and details)
notes: Use evidence to build an explanation relating an object's speed to its energy: a faster ball knocks a cup farther, a faster cart makes a louder bump. Energy is introduced as something a moving object has more of when it moves faster. Boundary: speed is compared (faster, slower), never calculated, and energy is not given a precise or number definition. A ramp's height is only a way to get more speed; stored energy of position is not taught or tested (4-PS3-1 evidence statement). Assumes from s3-motion-patterns the habit of describing motion by how far and how fast. Comes first in grade 4 physical science, with s4-collisions beside it; s4-energy-transfer then follows energy as it moves.

words: energy; transfer; heat; light; sound; electric current; circuit; battery; conductor
notes: Make observations that give evidence energy moves from place to place by sound (a drum makes rice on another drum jump), light (sunlight warms a dark cloth), heat (a warm hand warms a cold spoon) and electric current (a battery, wires and a bulb or buzzer in a closed circuit). Extends the energy transfer model that s4-collisions starts: a drawing with arrows that follows energy from where it starts to where it goes, now through sound, light, heat and current. Boundary: no number measurements of energy. Teacher note: use only low-voltage batteries; never household outlets; a battery wired straight to itself (a short circuit) gets hot, so the bulb or buzzer is always in the loop; no lenses aimed at skin. Hands on to s5-food-energy-sun, where the arrows follow energy from the sun into food. Across bands it assumes sk-sun-warms (kindergarten: sunlight warms surfaces; skips because grades 1 to 3 have no energy standard). Handoff kind: from sk-sun-warms (kindergarten) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of sk-sun-warms.

words: collide; collision; energy; transfer; speed; predict; contact force
notes: Ask questions and predict outcomes about how energy changes when objects collide: a rolling marble hits a still one, a toy car hits a block, the faster one before the collision gives more motion, sound or warmth after. Emphasis is on the change in energy that comes with the change in speed, not on the forces; the force arrows of s3-balanced-forces appear only to show the push at contact that passes energy on. Boundary: no number measurements of energy. Teacher note: rolling objects at low speed, on the floor or a table edge guard; no throwing. Taught with s4-speed-energy, before s4-energy-transfer (reconcile 2026-11-13: OpenSciEd elementary runs collisions in 4.1 before electricity in 4.2, and the clarification ties this change in energy to the change in speed of 4-PS3-1). Introduces the energy transfer model here as a simple arrow: where the energy was before the crash and every place it went after (the pins, the sound, a little warmth); s4-energy-transfer then follows the same arrows through sound, light, heat and current.

words: device; convert; design; test; refine; prototype; criteria; constraint; stored energy
cross_subject: math:4.OA.A.3 (multistep word problems when a design has a budget of materials)
notes: Apply energy ideas to design, test and refine a device that changes energy from one form to another: a circuit that drives a small motor car, lights a bulb or sounds a buzzer; a rubber-band or spring car using stored energy; a passive solar heater (a box that turns sunlight into warmth). Before building, the class states the criteria (what the device must do) and the constraints (materials, cost and time) and compares first proposals against them: ETS1.A is secondary to 4-PS3-4 in the standard, so the problem-defining of s3-design-problem is used again here. This row starts 3-5-ETS1-3: students test their device, find where it fails and improve it, but without the planned fair test with controlled variables that s5-design-test completes. Boundary: devices change motion into electric energy or use stored energy to cause motion, light or sound. Teacher note: low-voltage batteries only, no outlets; watch for hot wires in a short circuit; solar heaters can get hot, use a thermometer, not a hand. Also hands on to s8-potential-energy, which names the stored energy of the rubber-band or spring car.

words: wave; amplitude; wavelength; peak; crest; trough; vibration; pattern
cross_subject: math:4.G.A.1 (drawing points, lines and line segments to mark a wave and its wavelength)
notes: Develop a model of waves (a drawing, a rope or slinky wave, a wave machine of straws and tape, ripples in a tray of water) to describe them by their patterns: amplitude (how tall) and wavelength (peak to peak), and to show that waves make things move (a floating cork bobs up and down but is not carried away). Introduces the wave model, built on K-2's sound and vibration work (1-PS4-1). Boundary: no interference, no light or other electromagnetic waves as waves, no single non-repeating waves, no number models of amplitude or wavelength. Teacher note: water trays on a covered table; wipe spills at once. Hands on to grade 8 sound waves (MS-PS4-1), across the band. Across bands it assumes s1-sound-vibrates (grade 1: sound comes from vibrating materials; skips because grades 2 and 3 have no sound or wave standard). Comes after the energy rows: a wave carries energy across (the cork bobs) while the water stays where it was; the standard connects 4-PS4-1 to the energy core ideas of 4-PS3, and sound was already one way energy moved in s4-energy-transfer. Handoff kind: from s1-sound-vibrates (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: light; reflect; eye; source; path; mirror; see; object
cross_subject: ela:SL.4.5 (adding a drawing or visual display to a spoken explanation)
notes: Develop a model that shows we see an object because light from a source bounces off the object and travels into the eye: drawn rays with arrows from lamp to object to eye, tested with mirrors, a flashlight in a box with a peephole and a dark room. The common idea that light goes out from the eye is tested and revised with evidence. Introduces the light-ray model (the arrows light follows, made more exact in grade 6; it is not a wave model at this grade). Boundary: not which colors are reflected, no cells of the eye or how the retina works. Teacher note: never look at the sun, even through a mirror; no lasers. Hands on to s5-star-brightness and to grade 6 light and matter (MS-PS4-2), across the band. Across bands it assumes s1-see-with-light (grade 1: objects are seen only when lit; skips because grades 2 and 3 have no light standard); s1-light-materials (grade 1: materials pass, block or reflect light; skips because grades 2 and 3 have no light standard). Links back to s4-energy-transfer: light carries energy from the source, so this row follows the energy rows. Taught first in the block with s4-senses-brain and s4-structures-function: the eye is the first sense organ the class meets. Handoff kind: from s1-see-with-light (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s1-light-materials (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: code; signal; pattern; information; transfer; Morse code; grid; pixel; compare; solution
cross_subject: math:4.OA.C.5 (making and following a pattern by a rule)
notes: Generate and compare several solutions that use patterns to send information: drum beats in a code across the field, a grid of 1s and 0s that sends a black and white picture, flashlight Morse code. Each team builds two or more codes and judges them against shared criteria (speed, errors, distance) and constraints. 3-5-ETS1-2 is done in full here: students produce more than one solution and compare how well each is likely to meet the criteria, building on the problem definition of s3-design-problem. s4-hazard-solutions uses the same comparison. Comes after s4-wave-model: sound signals can be described with that mechanical-wave model where useful. Students use patterns in sound or flashes of light to send information. They do not need a wave model of light. Across bands it assumes s1-signal-device (grade 1: a device that sends a message with light or sound; skips because grades 2 and 3 have no communication standard). Core idea to include (PS4.C): digitized information can be sent over long distances without losing quality, and phones and computers turn it into a pattern, send it and decode it back into voice or a picture; one short reading carries this. Handoff kind: from s1-signal-device (grade 1) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s2-compare-designs and s3-design-problem.

words: structure; function; internal; external; organ; heart; lung; stomach; brain; skin; root; stem; petal; thorn
cross_subject: ela:W.4.1 (an opinion piece supported by reasons and information)
notes: Construct an argument that plants and animals have internal and external structures that work to support survival, growth, behavior and reproduction: roots take in water, thorns protect, colored petals draw pollinators, the heart pumps blood, lungs take in air, skin protects. Each structure is part of a larger system in the body or plant. Assumes s3-life-cycles (reproduction as a stage the structures serve) and s3-variation-advantage (a difference in a structure can help survival). Boundary: structures that can be seen without a microscope; no cells. Hands on to s5-plant-matter the idea that leaves and roots take in materials, and to grade 6 cells and body systems (MS-LS1-3), across the band. Across bands it also assumes s1-parts-mimic (grade 1: outside parts help plants and animals survive, 1.LS1.A in the standard's articulation; skips because grades 2 and 3 have no structure standard). The argument judges whether the evidence offered is relevant and enough (the evidence statement), and the plant half is argued as fully as the animal half, with its own phenomenon. Handoff kind: from s1-parts-mimic (grade 1) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s3-variation-advantage.

words: sense; senses; brain; nerve; signal; information; respond; react; memory
cross_subject: ela:SL.4.5 (a visual display that makes an explanation clear)
notes: Use a model to describe how animals take in different kinds of information through their senses, process it in the brain and respond in different ways: a flow model from sense organ to brain to action, tested with reaction-time games (catching a dropped ruler) and examples from other animals (an owl hearing prey, a snake sensing heat). Emphasis on how information moves through a system. Boundary: not how the brain stores and recalls memories, nor how sense receptors work. Comes after s4-light-eye (the eye is the first sense organ met) and before s4-structures-function, which widens from the sense organs to all structures (reconcile judgment, 2026-11-13). Core idea to include (LS1.D): animals use their perceptions and memories to guide their actions, shown with a learned signal (a new clap pattern that comes to mean a set action, timed in early and late rounds); how the brain stores memories stays outside the boundary. Hands on to grade 6 (MS-LS1-8), across the band. Across bands it assumes s1-parts-mimic (grade 1: animals have parts that sense what is around them and respond, 1.LS1.D in the standard's articulation; skips because grades 2 and 3 have no senses standard). Handoff kind: from s1-parts-mimic (grade 1) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: rock layer; fossil; landscape; canyon; erosion; older; younger; change over time; evidence
cross_subject: ela:W.4.7 (a short research project that builds knowledge of a topic)
notes: Identify evidence from patterns in rock layers and the fossils in them to explain how a landscape changed over time: shell fossils in a layer above plant fossils show land became sea; a canyon with layered walls and a river at the bottom shows the river cut through the rock. Lower layers in undisturbed rock are older (relative time). Assumes s3-fossils (fossils show past organisms and environments). Boundary: not how rocks form, no memorizing named formations, relative time only. BASELINE rule 5: the great age of the Earth is stated as the evidence shows. Hands on to grade 6 rock cycling (MS-ESS1-4, MS-ESS2-2), across the band. Across bands it assumes s2-fast-slow-events (grade 2: land changes fast or slowly over time (stability-change); skips because grade 3 has no landform standard). stability-change carries: land that looks the same changes slowly, layer by layer. Comes after s4-weathering-erosion: the canyon in the clarification statement is a river cutting rock, which is erosion over a long time. Core idea to include (ESS1.C): earth forces such as earthquakes bend and break layers, so one case of bent or broken layers is read as evidence. Handoff kind: from s2-fast-slow-events (grade 2) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s3-fossils.

words: weathering; erosion; deposition; slope; sediment; rate; freeze; thaw; variable; measure
cross_subject: math:4.MD.A.1 (knowing relative sizes of units when measuring how far sediment moves)
notes: Make observations and measurements that give evidence of weathering, or of the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind or plants: a stream table or sloped tray of sand with the slope, water amount or plant cover changed one at a time; freezing and thawing a wet clay or plaster block; shaking rocks in a jar. Data go in tables and bar graphs, built on s3-weather-data. Boundary: one kind of weathering or erosion at a time. Weathering (breaking rock into smaller pieces) and erosion (carrying the pieces away) are two words and are never blurred in a lesson, item or answer key. Core ideas to include: rainfall shapes the land and affects what can live there (ESS2.A), and living things change the land around them, as roots crack rock and burrows move soil (ESS2.E). Teacher note: water and sand on covered tables; wash hands after handling soil. Hands on to s5-sphere-interactions (water and wind shaping land is two Earth systems interacting). Across bands it assumes s2-erosion-solutions (grade 2: wind and water change the shape of land; skips because grade 3 has no erosion standard). Across bands it also assumes s2-fast-slow-events (grade 2: some changes to land are fast and some slow, 2.ESS1.C in the standard's articulation; skips because grade 3 has no landform standard). Handoff kind: from s2-erosion-solutions (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s2-fast-slow-events (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: map; topographic; mountain; volcano; earthquake; ocean floor; continent; boundary; trench; pattern
cross_subject: ela:RI.4.7 (interpreting information shown in maps, charts and diagrams); social-studies:ss4-state-maps (reading physical maps of a state)
notes: Analyze and interpret maps to describe patterns in Earth's features: topographic maps of land and the ocean floor, and maps that place mountains, continental edges, volcanoes and earthquakes. The pattern to find: mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes line up in belts, often along the edges of continents, and the ocean floor has mountain ranges and trenches. No plate tectonics by name; the pattern is left as a question that grade 6 answers (MS-ESS2-3, the plate model), across the band. Hands on to s5-water-distribution the map reading of oceans, ice and land. Across bands it assumes s2-land-water-model (grade 2: a model or map of land and water in an area; skips because grade 3 has no map-of-Earth-features standard). Students first put the map data into a table or chart, then describe the pattern (the 4-ESS2-2 evidence statement). Across bands it also assumes s2-water-where (grade 2: where water is found on Earth, 2.ESS2.C in the standard's articulation; skips because grade 3 has no map-of-Earth-features standard). Handoff kind: from s2-land-water-model (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s2-water-where (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: natural resource; fuel; fossil fuel; renewable; nonrenewable; wind; solar; dam; pollution; environment
cross_subject: ela:W.4.8 (gathering information from print and digital sources and taking notes); social-studies:ss4-regions-resources (natural resources of US regions)
notes: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels come from natural resources and that using them affects the environment. Renewable: wind, water behind dams, sunlight. Nonrenewable: fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and the fuel used in nuclear power plants. Effects: habitat lost to dams and surface mines, air pollution from burning fossil fuels. Uses the energy transfer arrows from s4-energy-transfer. Taught right after s4-energy-device, opened by the question the device work raises: where does the current in the wall come from? (OpenSciEd elementary carries 4-ESS3-1 in its electricity unit, and the core idea says currents are often produced to begin with from the energy of motion.) Assumes s3-environment-change-solution (a change to the environment changes what lives there). Facts and backed sources decide claims (values rule b); no resource is cheered or blamed beyond what the evidence shows. Hands on to s5-protect-resources.

words: natural hazard; earthquake; flood; tsunami; volcano; eruption; warning; monitor; reduce; impact
cross_subject: ela:RI.4.9 (combining information from two texts on the same topic); social-studies:ss4-disasters-response (how communities respond to disasters)
notes: Generate and compare several solutions that reduce the effects of natural Earth processes on people: an earthquake-resistant building (tested on a shake table of a tray and rubber balls), better monitoring of a volcano, tsunami warnings, flood walls. Builds on s3-weather-hazard (judging one solution) by producing and comparing several, as s4-information-codes taught; uses s4-earth-feature-maps to see where hazards cluster. Boundary: earthquakes, floods, tsunamis and volcanic eruptions only. Teacher note: some students may have lived through a disaster; keep examples general and let students choose whether to share. Hands on to s5-design-test. Across bands it assumes s2-erosion-solutions (grade 2: comparing designs that reduce the effects of Earth processes; skips because grade 3 has no landform-process standard). Comes after s4-weathering-erosion and s4-earth-feature-maps: a flood plan can be tested on the erosion tray, where moving water carrying land away is already known (reconcile judgment, 2026-11-13). Handoff kind: from s2-erosion-solutions (grade 2) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s3-weather-hazard.

words: matter; particle; too small to see; gas; air; dissolve; evaporate; compress; model
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.7 (drawing on several print and digital sources to answer a question)
notes: Develop a model that matter is made of particles too small to be seen, from evidence the class gathers: pumping air into a ball makes it firmer and heavier; air in a closed syringe can be squeezed; sugar dissolved in water vanishes from sight but the water tastes sweet; salt water left to dry leaves salt behind. Introduces the particle model (dots drawn for parts too small to see, closer or farther apart) and the idea of very small scale. Students revise their first drawings as each piece of evidence arrives. Boundary: no atoms or molecules by name, no particle-level account of evaporation and condensation. Teacher note: never taste in the lab; the teacher does any tasting demonstration with food-safe materials, or it is described. Hands on to grade 6 thermal energy (MS-PS1-4), across the band. Across bands it assumes s2-pieces-new-object (grade 2: an object built from small pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt; skips because grades 3 and 4 have no matter standard). Handoff kind: from s2-pieces-new-object (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: weight; conserve; total; scale; gram; melt; freeze; dissolve; mix; before; after
cross_subject: math:5.MD.A.1 (converting grams and kilograms within one system)
notes: Measure and graph weights to give evidence that when substances are heated, cooled or mixed, the total weight stays the same, whatever the change: ice melting in a sealed bag, salt dissolving in water, baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bottle with a balloon on top. Data go in a before and after table and bar graph; a change in weight is traced to something escaping (a gas), which the particle model explains. Boundary: mass and weight are not told apart. Teacher note: eye protection for any fizzing mix; seal only with a balloon or loose cap, never a tight lid, so pressure cannot build. Comes after s5-particles. Across bands it assumes s2-pieces-new-object (grade 2: the same pieces make a new whole, nothing lost; skips because grades 3 and 4 have no matter standard). Handoff kind: from s2-pieces-new-object (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: property; material; hardness; color; reflect; conduct; magnetic; dissolve; solubility; identify
cross_subject: ela:W.5.8 (recording information and summarizing it in notes)
notes: Make observations and measurements to identify materials by their properties: white powders (baking soda, cornstarch, sugar, salt), metals, minerals and liquids, tested for color, hardness, shine, whether they conduct electricity or heat, whether a magnet pulls them and whether they dissolve. Students build a property table and use its pattern to name an unknown sample. Boundary: density is not used as a property; mass and weight are not told apart. Teacher note: eye protection; no tasting; powders kept from the eyes and mouth; wash hands after. Builds on K-2's sorting by property (2-PS1-1), across the band. Across bands it assumes s2-material-properties (grade 2: describing and sorting materials by observable properties; skips because grades 3 and 4 have no matter standard). Also assumes s2-best-material (grade 2: testing materials to match their properties to a purpose). Handoff kind: from s2-material-properties (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s2-best-material (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: mix; mixture; new substance; change; gas; bubbles; property; evidence
cross_subject: ela:W.5.7 (a short research project using several sources)
notes: Conduct an investigation to decide whether mixing two or more substances makes a new substance: new properties (bubbles of a new gas, a color change, a solid forming, warmth) are evidence of a new substance, while a mixture that can be separated again (sand and salt, iron filings and sand) is not. Students plan which mixes to test and what counts as evidence. Comes after s5-identify-materials so properties are known tools. Teacher note: eye protection for all mixing; only kitchen-safe substances (baking soda, vinegar, milk, lemon juice, cornstarch, steel wool and water), never household cleaners; no tasting. Hands on to grade 7 chemical reactions (MS-PS1-2), across the band. Across bands it assumes s2-heat-cool-change (grade 2: changes that can and cannot be reversed; skips because grades 3 and 4 have no matter standard). Also hands on to s7-synthetic-materials. Handoff kind: from s2-heat-cool-change (grade 2) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: gravity; force; down; center; Earth; sphere; pull; argument
cross_subject: ela:W.5.1 (opinion writing supported by logically ordered reasons)
notes: Support an argument that Earth's gravity pulls objects down, where down means toward the center of the round Earth: plumb lines and dropped objects everywhere fall toward the ground, and on a globe that is toward the middle, so 'down' in Australia points a different way in space than 'down' here. Force arrows from s3-balanced-forces now point toward Earth's center. Assumes s3-balanced-forces (gravity as a pull down, force arrows) and s3-magnet-static (a pull without touching); both skip grade 4 because grade 4 teaches no forces standard. Boundary: no math for gravity. Hands on to grade 8 forces at a distance (MS-PS2-4), across the band. Also hands on to s8-potential-energy (energy stored by height). Handoff kind: from s3-balanced-forces (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s3-magnet-static (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: energy; food; sun; sunlight; plant; animal; body warmth; growth; flow chart
cross_subject: ela:SL.5.5 (adding visual displays to a presentation)
notes: Use models (diagrams, flow charts) to describe that the energy in animals' food, used for growth, repair, motion and keeping warm, was once energy from the sun: sun to grass to cow to person, each arrow an energy transfer. Uses the energy transfer arrows of s4-energy-transfer and the food web drawn in s5-matter-movement, and keeps energy (which flows through) apart from matter (which cycles). No photosynthesis chemistry. Hands on to grade 7 matter and energy in organisms (MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3), across the band. Also hands on to s7-photosynthesis, where light energy is stored in sugar.

words: plant; matter; growth; air; water; soil; carbon dioxide; argument; evidence
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.9 (combining information from several texts on one topic); math:5.MD.A.1 (comparing weights in grams and kilograms)
notes: Support an argument that plants get the materials they need to grow chiefly from air and water, not from soil: the historical tree-in-a-pot data (soil weight barely changes while the tree gains many kilograms), plants grown in water alone, and the class's own weighed soil before and after. The particle model of s5-particles makes air a kind of matter that can become plant. Assumes s3-environment-traits (plants grown short of water are stunted) and s4-structures-function (roots and leaves take in materials). Emphasis is on where plant matter comes from; light is the energy, not the material. Teacher note: check allergies to plants, soil and mold. Comes after s5-particles. The handoff from s3-environment-traits skips grade 4 because grade 4 has no plant-growth standard. Hands on to s7-photosynthesis, which explains with atoms how air and water become plant matter. structure-function carries from s4-structures-function: roots and leaves are the structures that take in the water and air that become plant matter. Handoff kind: from s3-environment-traits (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: ecosystem; producer; consumer; decomposer; food web; matter; cycle; soil; nutrient; environment
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.7 (drawing on several sources to answer a question)
notes: Develop a model of matter moving among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment: plants make food from air and water; animals eat plants or other animals; decomposers break dead matter into soil, air and water that plants use again. Introduces the food web (who eats whom, with decomposers) and the matter cycle (matter goes round and is used again); a sealed jar ecosystem or a compost bottle gives first-hand evidence over weeks. Assumes s3-habitat-survival (a habitat as a system whose parts depend on each other), a skip because grade 4 has no ecosystem standard. Boundary: no molecules. Teacher note: keep compost bottles closed; wash hands; mold allergies. Hands on to grade 7 matter cycling and ecosystems (MS-LS2-3), across the band. Also hands on to s7-photosynthesis, s7-ecosystem-disruption and s7-interaction-patterns, which all reuse the food web. Handoff kind: from s3-habitat-survival (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: shadow; length; direction; day; night; rotate; orbit; season; star; constellation; pattern
cross_subject: math:5.G.A.2 (graphing points on the coordinate plane to show how a shadow changes over a day)
notes: Represent data in graphs to reveal daily and seasonal patterns: a shadow stick's shadow measured each hour (length and direction), day length through the year, and stars or constellations seen only in some months. Introduces the Earth-sun-moon model as Earth spinning (day and night, moving shadows) and moving around the sun (different night-sky stars by season), checked with a globe and lamp. Boundary: the causes of seasons are not taught (grade 8, MS-ESS1-1). Teacher note: never look at the sun, even briefly or through tinted glass. Across bands it assumes s1-sky-patterns (grade 1: predictable patterns of sun, moon and stars; skips because grades 2 to 4 have no sky standard); s1-daylight-seasons (grade 1: day length changes through the year; skips because grades 2 to 4 have no sky standard). Handoff kind: from s1-sky-patterns (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s1-sky-patterns. Handoff kind: from s1-daylight-seasons (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s1-daylight-seasons.

words: star; sun; brightness; apparent; distance; near; far; light year
cross_subject: math:5.NBT.A.2 (powers of ten for very large distances)
notes: Support an argument that the sun looks far brighter than other stars because it is much closer to Earth: two equal flashlights at different distances in a dark hall give evidence, and star distance data in powers of ten show the scale. Uses the light-ray model of s4-light-eye (light from the star travels to the eye; less of it arrives from farther away). The sun is a star. Boundary: relative distance only; not star size, mass, age or stage. Comes after s5-shadows-sky. Hands on to grade 8 Earth in space (MS-ESS1-3), across the band.

words: geosphere; hydrosphere; atmosphere; biosphere; system; interact; climate; landform; ocean
cross_subject: ela:SL.5.5 (a visual display in a presentation)
notes: Develop a model, through one worked example, of how two of Earth's systems interact: the ocean shapes coastlines and local climate and supports life; rain and wind wear down land; mountains force air up so clouds form on one side. Each of rock and land, water, air and living things is a system. Assumes s4-weathering-erosion (water and wind change land) and s3-climates (climate regions, a skip since grade 4 has no climate standard). Boundary: two systems at a time. Hands on to grade 6 weather, climate and water cycling (MS-ESS2-4, MS-ESS2-6), across the band. Handoff kind: from s3-climates (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: salt water; fresh water; ocean; glacier; ice cap; groundwater; lake; river; percent; reservoir
cross_subject: math:4.NF.C.6 (hundredths as decimals, for the share of Earth's water in each place)
notes: Describe and graph how much of Earth's water is salt water and how much is fresh, and where the fresh water is: about 97 of every 100 parts in the ocean, most fresh water locked in glaciers and ice caps or underground, and very little in lakes and rivers. A bar graph and a hundred-square grid make the scale visible. Assumes s4-earth-feature-maps (reading maps of oceans and ice). Boundary: oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, groundwater and polar ice only; water in the air is not included. Comes after s5-sphere-interactions. Hands on to s5-protect-resources the case that usable fresh water is scarce. Across bands it assumes s2-water-where (grade 2: where water is found on Earth, solid or liquid; skips because grades 3 and 4 have no water standard). Shares are said as parts out of 100 on the hundred-square grid and the bar graph; percent is named as another way to say out of 100, with no percent calculations (those are grade 6, 6.RP.A.3c). Handoff kind: from s2-water-where (grade 2) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s4-earth-feature-maps.

words: resource; protect; conserve; pollution; community; recycle; habitat; solution
cross_subject: ela:W.5.8 (gathering information from print and digital sources)
notes: Obtain and combine information about how communities use science ideas to protect Earth's resources and environment: protecting watersheds, cleaning up runoff, restoring wetlands, cutting air pollution, saving water. Students connect each action to the Earth system it protects. Assumes s4-energy-resources (using resources affects the environment). Uses the fresh water case from s5-water-distribution. Facts and backed sources decide claims (values rule b). Supplies the design problem for s5-design-test. Hands on to grade 7 human impact (MS-ESS3-3), across the band. Also hands on to s7-population-consumption and s7-biodiversity-solutions.

words: fair test; variable; control; trial; failure point; prototype; improve; criteria; constraint
cross_subject: math:5.MD.B.2 (line plots of repeated measurements in fractions of a unit)
notes: The band's full design cycle, completing 3-5-ETS1-3: define a problem from s5-protect-resources (for example a filter that cleans muddy water, or a device that catches rain runoff), generate and compare solutions, then plan and run fair tests of the prototype in which one variable changes and the rest are held the same, with several trials, and find the failure points that show what to improve. s4-energy-device started this standard by testing and refining a device; here the fair test is planned and the data are graphed before a change is made. Assumes s4-energy-device, s4-information-codes and s4-hazard-solutions. Teacher note: filtered water is never drunk; gloves for muddy or runoff water; wash hands. Hands on to grade 6 to 8 engineering (MS-ETS1-3, MS-ETS1-4), across the band.
