words: light source; reflect; transmit; absorb; refract; ray; transparent; translucent; opaque; receptor
cross_subject: math:5.NBT.A.1 (light-sensor readings that differ by factors of ten); math:6.SP.A.2 (repeated readings described by center and spread, guided)
notes: Base unit 6.1 (one-way mirror). Light travels from a source in straight lines until it meets a material; there it is reflected, transmitted or (with s6-insulator-design) absorbed, depending on the material, and its path bends where it crosses from one transparent material into another (air to water, air to glass). We see an object only when light from it enters the eye, so a one-way mirror works because far more light reaches one side than the other. Students draw and revise ray diagrams (the light-ray model, carried from s4-light-eye in grade 4 and made more exact here with absorption and bending) and test them with flashlights, mirrors and films. Contributing row for MS-PS4-2: the base text builds this PE across 6.1, 6.2, 8.2 and 8.4 (the 6.1 unit page marks it partial and calls 6.1 the first unit of the sequence), so the PE is not complete here. Grade 6 assesses only the ray-model part: light reflected, absorbed or transmitted by materials and bending where it crosses between transparent materials. s8-wave-amplitude-energy assesses the sound half and s8-earth-sun-moon assesses the light-wave model (brightness, color, frequency-dependent bending, light crossing empty space). The code sits on this row only because every row must name a standard and every PE is owned in one grade; moving the owner to grade 8 waits on a way to mark contributing rows. Also starts MS-LS1-8 (owned by s8-senses-brain): the eye has receptors that respond to light and send signals to the brain. Boundary: qualitative only; no wave equations, no lens formulas. Teacher note: no laser pointers into eyes; flashlights or low-power class 2 lasers only, beam kept below eye level. Across bands it assumes s4-light-eye (grade 4: light from a source reflects off objects into the eye (light-ray); skips because grade 5 has no light-and-matter standard). Math: if light-sensor readings are used, readings that differ by powers of ten lean on 5.NBT.A.1, and describing repeated readings by center and spread is guided, since grade 6 math teaches 6.SP.A.2 in the same year. Load: contributing row (unit 6.1; MS-PS4-2 is finished in grade 8). Handoff kind: from s4-light-eye (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Contributes to MS-PS4-2 (marked ~): the ray part is done here; s8-earth-sun-moon (unit 8.4) owns and completes it with the wave model of light, as the 6.1 and 8.4 teacher editions place it.

hands_on: s7-reactions-atoms; s7-reaction-energy; s8-kinetic-energy-graphs; chem-reaction-rates; chem-thermal-equilibrium; chem-equilibrium-design; chem-energy-accounting; s8-energy-transfer-argument
words: particle; kinetic energy; temperature; thermal energy; energy transfer; mass; variable; control
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (temperature against time as two quantities that change together)
notes: Base unit 6.2 (double-walled cup). Matter is made of particles always in motion; temperature measures the average kinetic energy of those particles, and energy moves from the warmer sample to the cooler one through collisions until they match. Students plan and run fair tests of how the energy transferred depends on the type of matter, the mass and the temperature change (ice melting in different amounts of water; equal masses of different materials cooling), choosing what to vary, hold steady and measure, then graph temperature against time. Heat is used in its science sense, energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Also develops MS-PS3-5 in full, since the 6.2 unit page lists it without the partial mark and the scope and sequence names no other unit for it: students build an evidence-supported argument, with a before and after energy account, that when the particles of a sample speed up or slow down, energy has been transferred to or from it. The code sits on s8-energy-transfer-argument, the later application, because every row must name a standard and each PE is owned in one grade. Boundary: no calculation of the total energy transferred. Teacher note: hot water no hotter than a tap or kettle-cooled 60 C, kept by the teacher; spills wiped at once. Across bands it assumes s5-particles (grade 5: matter made of particles too small to see); s4-energy-transfer (grade 4: energy moves from place to place by heat; skips because grade 5 energy is food energy, not heat). Also hands on to chem-equilibrium-design and chem-energy-accounting. Load: development row (unit 6.2). Handoff kind: from s4-energy-transfer (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Also owns MS-PS3-5: unit 6.2 develops it in full; s8-energy-transfer-argument applies it to whole objects.

words: conduction; convection; radiation; insulator; conductor; criteria; constraints; prototype; system; boundary
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.5 (summarize repeated trial data with a measure of center)
notes: Base unit 6.2. Students apply what they found about particle collisions, moving air or water carrying energy, and light being absorbed (the absorbed part of MS-PS4-2) to design, build and test a cup or container that keeps a drink cold longest, against criteria (temperature change over a set time) and constraints (cost, materials, size). Each design is drawn as a system with a boundary, with arrows for energy moving in or out. Students test, compare and revise. Also starts MS-ETS1-4 (owned by s7-design-optimize): a model is used to predict and test design changes before building. Boundary: no calculation of energy transferred. Teacher note: as for s6-particle-temperature; no glass containers for student-built designs. Across bands it assumes s5-design-test (grade 5: fair tests of prototypes against criteria). Load: development row (unit 6.2).

words: solid; liquid; gas; melting; freezing; evaporation; condensation; state; pure substance
cross_subject: math:6.NS.C.5 (temperatures below zero as negative numbers)
notes: Base unit 6.3 (hail falling on warm days). Particle drawings of solids (close, vibrating in place), liquids (touching, sliding past) and gases (far apart, colliding) are used to predict what happens when thermal energy is added or removed: the particles speed up or slow down until the substance changes state, and the same particles remain. Students explain condensation on a cold can and freezing water drops high in a storm cloud. Completes MS-PS1-4, which s6-particle-temperature started. Examples: water, carbon dioxide (dry ice, teacher handled), helium. Boundary: qualitative molecular models; no latent heat values. Teacher note: dry ice only with gloves and tongs by the teacher, never sealed in a container. Across bands it assumes s5-conserve-weight (grade 5: matter is conserved through changes). Load: completion row (unit 6.3, finishing work begun in 6.2).

words: water cycle; evaporation; condensation; precipitation; runoff; groundwater; humidity; gravity
notes: Base unit 6.3. Water moves through ocean, air, land, ice and living things on many paths, changing state as it goes. Energy from the sun drives evaporation and lifts water vapor; gravity pulls precipitation, runoff and groundwater downhill. Students build a model from their particle and energy ideas and use it to trace how water reaches a hailstorm and returns to the ground. Introduces the water-cycle model at middle school depth. Boundary: latent heat is not treated with numbers. Across bands it assumes s5-sphere-interactions (grade 5: Earth systems interact (water, air, land)); s5-water-distribution (grade 5: where water is on Earth and how much). Load: development row (unit 6.3).

words: air mass; air pressure; front; humidity; wind; forecast; probability; weather
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (pressure and temperature against time)
notes: Base unit 6.3. Air flows from high pressure to low pressure; where warm, moist air rises and cools, clouds and storms form, and where different air masses meet (a front) the weather can change suddenly. Students collect or are given temperature, pressure, humidity and wind data and weather maps, find patterns, and say what weather is likely at a place, as a range of chances, not a certainty. Boundary: students are not asked to recall cloud names or weather-map symbols. Across bands it assumes s5-sphere-interactions (grade 5: air and water interact to make weather); s3-weather-data (grade 3: weather data read for patterns; skips because grades 4 and 5 have no weather standard). Hands on to chem-earth-energy-climate, where the same air and water movements are read as energy flowing through Earth's systems (HS-ESS2-4). Load: development row (unit 6.3). Handoff kind: from s3-weather-data (grade 3) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s4-weathering-erosion and s5-sphere-interactions.

words: climate; latitude; altitude; prevailing wind; ocean current; uneven heating; rotation; salinity; density
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-mena-maps (latitude bands on a map)
notes: Base unit 6.3, second anchor (regional rain patterns). Climate is the long-run pattern of weather. Sunlight heats the Earth unevenly by latitude (sunlight strike the poles at a low angle, reusing the earth-sun-moon model from earlier grades), so air and ocean water circulate in large loops; the Earth's rotation turns winds and currents into steady patterns (prevailing winds, ocean currents carrying warm water toward the poles). With mountains, distance from the ocean and altitude, these explain why regions have the climates they do. Boundary: the Coriolis effect is named and its result used; its dynamics are not taught. Across bands it assumes s3-climates (grade 3: climates of different regions; skips because grades 4 and 5 have no climate standard); s5-shadows-sky (grade 5: the earth-sun-moon model (sun angle and day length)). Students develop, revise and use a linked atmosphere-ocean model to explain a regional climate. Include density differences caused by temperature and salinity, heat redistribution, rotation and continental boundaries that steer ocean currents. Do not derive Coriolis dynamics. Load: development row (unit 6.3). Handoff kind: from s3-climates (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: rock cycle; igneous; sedimentary; metamorphic; weathering; erosion; deposition; magma; crystallization
notes: Base unit 6.4 (Mount Everest rising). Earth materials cycle: melting, crystallization, weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction and deformation turn rocks from one kind into another. Energy from the Earth's hot interior drives melting and uplift; energy from the sun drives the water and wind that weather and carry rock. Students build the rock-cycle model and trace how marine rock ends up near the top of a mountain. Boundary: no naming of minerals. Across bands it assumes s4-weathering-erosion (grade 4: weathering and erosion by water, ice and wind; skips because grade 5 has no rock standard). stability-change carries from grade 4 (s4-rock-layers, s4-weathering-erosion): grade 5 has no standard whose crosscutting concept is stability and change, so the model rests there. The rock cycle is change at every scale inside an Earth that looks stable. Load: development row (unit 6.4). Handoff kind: from s4-weathering-erosion (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Reactivation: stability-change was last used in grade 4 and is not used in grade(s) 5, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the stability-change model again before the new work.

words: uplift; landslide; glacier; time scale; gradual; catastrophic; landform
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.3b (rates such as millimeters per year)
notes: Base unit 6.4. Processes shape the surface at very different speeds and sizes: plates move a few centimeters a year and mountains rise over millions of years, while a landslide or eruption changes a slope in minutes. Students compare rates and explain a landform, choosing a local one where possible, as the sum of slow change punctuated by sudden events. The reasoning that grows is scale: a tiny rate over a huge time makes a huge change. Across bands it assumes s4-rock-layers (grade 4: rock layers record landscape change; skips because grade 5 has no landform standard). Load: development row (unit 6.4). Handoff kind: from s4-rock-layers (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: plate; plate tectonics; continent; seafloor; ridge; trench; fossil; evidence
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.3b (spreading rate as distance per year)
notes: Base unit 6.4. Students analyze maps of matching fossils and rocks across oceans, the fit of continental shelves, and the ridges and trenches on the seafloor, and argue that the plates have moved and are still moving. They build the plate model (plates moving apart, together and past each other) and use it to explain mountains such as the Himalaya. Boundary: magnetic striping of the seafloor is not assessed. Across bands it assumes s4-earth-feature-maps (grade 4: patterns of mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes on maps; skips because grade 5 has no landform standard). Load: development row (unit 6.4). Handoff kind: from s4-earth-feature-maps (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: rock layer; strata; relative age; geologic time scale; fossil; superposition; billion
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-timeline-deep-time (scaled timeline of deep time); math:6.RP.A.3 (scale 4.6 billion years to a timeline length)
notes: Base unit 6.4. Rock layers and the fossils in them are read in order (lower layers formed first unless the rocks were disturbed) to put events in sequence; the geologic time scale organizes the Earth's 4.6-billion-year history, from the formation of the Earth and the earliest life to the last ice age. Students build a scaled timeline and place mountain building, extinctions and eruptions on it. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5): the age of the Earth is stated plainly. Boundary: no recall of the names of periods or epochs. Across bands it assumes s4-rock-layers (grade 4: relative age from rock layers and fossils; skips because grade 5 has no rock or fossil standard). claim-evidence-reasoning: MS-ESS1-4 asks for a scientific explanation built from rock-strata evidence. Math: the timeline scale is provided (for example 1 meter for each billion years) until students can set a scale by ratio reasoning (6.RP.A.3), which grade 6 math teaches. Load: development row (unit 6.4). Handoff kind: from s4-rock-layers (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: natural hazard; earthquake; tsunami; forecast; mitigate; warning system; magnitude; frequency
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.4 (histograms of magnitudes and frequencies)
notes: Base unit 6.5 (the 2011 Japan earthquake and tsunami). Students map where and how often earthquakes, eruptions, tsunamis and storms happen, and use the plate model to explain the pattern. Some hazards give warning signs that allow forecasts (eruptions, hurricanes); earthquakes do not yet. They use the data to judge which technologies reduce harm (sea walls, warning buoys, evacuation routes, building design). Also starts MS-ETS1-1 (owned by s7-define-design-problem) and MS-ETS1-2 (owned by s8-design-evaluate): students state criteria and constraints for a tsunami-safety solution and compare two options. Teacher note: loss of life is discussed with care; some students may have lived through a disaster, so the unit uses data and design, not graphic images, and gives a way to step out. Across bands it assumes s4-hazard-solutions (grade 4: solutions that reduce the effects of natural hazards; skips because grade 5 has no hazard standard). Load: development row (unit 6.5). Handoff kind: from s4-hazard-solutions (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: signal; analog; digital; encode; transmit; noise; reliable
cross_subject: ela:RI.6.7 (integrate information from text, images and video)
notes: Base unit 6.5, lesson added in 2022 (alert systems). Waves can carry information. Students read and watch how warning systems changed from sirens and analog radio to digital alerts, and support the claim that digital signals are more reliable: a pattern of on and off pulses can be copied and re-sent without the small errors that build up in an analog signal. Boundary: no binary counting and no workings of any particular device. The wave-model carried here is the pulse or wave as a carrier of a pattern; amplitude and energy wait for s8-wave-amplitude-energy. Across bands it assumes s4-information-codes (grade 4: patterns that carry information; skips because grade 5 has no waves or information standard); s4-wave-model (grade 4: waves of amplitude and wavelength; skips because grade 5 has no waves standard). wave-model rests in grade 5 (from s4-wave-model): grade 5 has no waves standard. Load: development row, short (one added lesson in unit 6.5). Handoff kind: from s4-information-codes (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s4-wave-model (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Reactivation: wave-model was last used in grade 4 and is not used in grade(s) 5, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the wave-model model again before the new work.

words: cell; organism; unicellular; multicellular; microscope; tissue; organ; cell membrane; cell wall; nerve
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.1 (magnification as a ratio)
notes: Base unit 6.6 (a student breaks two bones in his foot). Students use microscopes and images to gather evidence that all living things are made of cells, one or many, and that cells tell living from non-living things. Also starts three PEs completed later: MS-LS1-2 (cell membrane and cell wall control what enters and leaves; owned by s8-cell-parts-function), MS-LS1-3 (cells form tissues and organs that work together in healing: skeletal, muscular, circulatory, nervous; owned by s7-body-systems-food) and MS-LS1-8 (nerve cells carry signals from receptors to the brain, felt as touch and pain; owned by s8-senses-brain). Teacher note: no human body fluids or cheek-cell swabs; prepared slides, plant and pond samples; glass slides and coverslips handled by the edges; the injury case is described without graphic images. Across bands it assumes s4-structures-function (grade 4: internal and external structures with functions; skips because grade 5 has no structure standard); s4-senses-brain (grade 4: senses send information to the brain; skips because grade 5 has no senses standard). structure-function carries from grade 5 (s5-plant-matter: roots and leaves take in materials). Load: development row (unit 6.6). Handoff kind: from s4-structures-function (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s4-senses-brain (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: substance; property; atom; molecule; chemical reaction; reactant; product; conservation of matter; mass; extended structure
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.1 (ratios of atoms in a molecule)
notes: Base unit 7.1 (a bath bomb fizzing away). Each pure substance has properties (density, melting point, solubility, odor, flammability) that identify it; substances are made of atoms joined into molecules; in a chemical reaction the atoms of the starting substances regroup into new molecules with new properties, and the number of each kind of atom stays the same, so mass is conserved (shown by weighing a reaction in a closed bag). Completes MS-PS1-2 here: students compare the permitted properties (density, melting point, solubility, odor, flammability) of substances before and after they interact to decide whether a reaction happened (the scope and sequence places this in 7.1, and the 7.3 teacher edition treats it as already developed). Starts MS-PS1-1 with models of simple molecules and one extended structure (a salt crystal), which s7-food-molecules completes with molecules of thousands of atoms. Also starts MS-LS1-8 (smell receptors respond to molecules; owned by s8-senses-brain). Boundary: no atomic masses, no balancing of symbolic equations, no bonding forces. Teacher note: eye protection for all mixing; citric acid and baking soda only; no tasting; closed bags vented away from faces. Also hands on to chem-equilibrium-design. Load: development row (unit 7.1).

words: release energy; absorb energy; exothermic; endothermic; concentration; surroundings
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (temperature against time for each reaction)
notes: Base unit 7.2 (the flameless heater in a field ration). Some reactions release energy to their surroundings and some take it in; the temperature of the system tells which. Students explain this with the particle model and design, test and modify a homemade heater or cold pack, varying the type and amount of substance. Boundary: criteria limited to amount, time and temperature. Teacher note: eye protection and gloves; calcium chloride and ammonium chloride only, in small amounts, never tasted; the field-ration heater is a teacher demonstration in a ventilated room, since it gives off hydrogen and gets very hot. Load: development row (unit 7.2).

words: optimize; iterate; model; test; trade-off; variable
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.2a (is the temperature change proportional to the amount used)
notes: Base unit 7.2. Students use a model (a small-scale test, a table of earlier results, a simple simulation) to generate data, change one variable at a time, and modify the heater design step by step toward the best result within the constraints. Completes MS-ETS1-4, started in s6-insulator-design. Also builds MS-ETS1-2 and MS-ETS1-3, owned by grade 8 rows, by comparing designs against criteria and combining the best features. Teacher note: as for s7-reaction-energy. Load: completion row (unit 7.2, finishing work begun in 6.2).

words: carbohydrate; starch; sugar; protein; fat; extended structure; digestion; indicator
cross_subject: math:6.NS.C.8 (graph digestion data on a coordinate grid); math:6.RP.A.2 (rates such as amount broken down per minute)
notes: Base unit 7.3 (a student with stomach pain and weight loss). Completes MS-PS1-1, started in s7-reactions-atoms, by extending molecular models to large molecules and extended structures; applies and extends MS-PS1-2, which s7-reactions-atoms completes in 7.1. Food is made of large molecules (starch, proteins, fats) with repeating subunits, and simple molecules (sugars, water); students model molecules of very different sizes (a scale idea: a starch molecule holds thousands of atoms, a water molecule three) and extended structures (a salt crystal, starch). They read data before and after digestion to see that large molecules are broken into smaller ones the body can use. The starch and sugar indicator tests are an application and extension of MS-PS1-2, not its proficiency evidence, which comes from the permitted properties compared in s7-reactions-atoms. Boundary: properties limited to density, melting and boiling point, solubility, flammability and odor; no valence electrons or full atom-by-atom drawings of large molecules. Teacher note: indicator solutions (iodine, glucose strips) with eye protection; no tasting; the case is about a real health condition, discussed without asking students about their own. Across bands it assumes s5-new-substances (grade 5: mixing can make a new substance with new properties; skips because grade 6 (base text order) has no chemical reactions unit); s5-identify-materials (grade 5: identifying substances by their properties; skips because grade 6 (base text order) has no chemical reactions unit). Load: completion and application row (unit 7.3, extending 7.1). Handoff kind: from s5-new-substances (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s5-identify-materials (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: subsystem; digestive system; circulatory system; respiratory system; excretory system; tissue; organ
cross_subject: ela:W.7.1 (written argument with evidence)
notes: Base unit 7.3. Completes MS-LS1-3, started in s6-cells-body-systems. Students argue from evidence how the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, excretory and muscular systems work together to get food molecules and oxygen to every cell and take wastes away, and what goes wrong when one part (the small intestine lining) is damaged. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems. Boundary: limited to these six systems with the nervous system; no mechanism of one system studied alone. Load: completion row (unit 7.3, finishing work begun in 6.6).

words: cellular respiration; glucose; oxygen; carbon dioxide; energy release; growth; repair; mitochondria
notes: Base unit 7.3. Inside cells, food molecules are broken apart and rebuilt: some atoms are rearranged into new molecules the body uses to grow and repair, and some molecules react with oxygen, releasing energy and giving off carbon dioxide and water. Students model the matter moving through the body and the energy released. Boundary: no details of the chemical reactions of respiration; no named intermediate molecules. Words: mitochondria is named here as the cell part where food molecules react with oxygen (the 7.4 part of MS-LS1-2 uses it next); grade 8 reuses the word. Load: development row (unit 7.3). Reactivation: matter-cycle was last used in grade 5 and is not used in grade(s) 6, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the matter-cycle model again before the new work.

words: photosynthesis; chloroplast; producer; glucose; carbon dioxide; light energy; sap
cross_subject: ela:W.7.2 (written scientific explanation)
notes: Base unit 7.4 (where maple syrup and breakfast foods come from). Plants take in carbon dioxide and water and, using light energy in their chloroplasts, rearrange the atoms into sugars and give off oxygen; most of a tree's mass comes from the air. Students explain from evidence (plant mass data, gas measurements) how photosynthesis moves matter and energy into organisms. Starts the 7.4 part of MS-LS1-2 (chloroplasts and mitochondria; owned by s8-cell-parts-function). Boundary: no biochemical steps of photosynthesis. Teacher note: tasting of syrup or sap only under the school's food policy and with allergy checks. Builds on grade 5: plants get their matter chiefly from air and water (s5-plant-matter), matter moves through the food web (s5-matter-movement) and the energy in food came from the sun (s5-food-energy-sun); the standard's articulation names 5.LS1.C, 5.LS2.A, 5.LS2.B and 5.PS3.D. Load: development row (unit 7.4). Handoff kind: from s5-plant-matter (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s5-matter-movement (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s5-food-energy-sun (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: natural resource; synthetic; material; process; impact; society
cross_subject: ela:W.7.8 (gather information from several sources)
notes: Base unit 7.4. Natural resources (plants, oil, minerals) are changed by chemical processes into synthetic materials such as plastics, medicines, fuels and sweeteners. Students gather and weigh information on one material: what it is made from, what reaction changes it, and how it helps and harms people and places. Boundary: qualitative only. Builds on s5-new-substances: mixing substances can make a new substance with new properties, now named as a chemical process. Load: development row, short (unit 7.4). Handoff kind: from s5-new-substances (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: ecosystem; producer; consumer; decomposer; food web; matter cycle; energy flow; system boundary
notes: Base unit 7.4. Matter cycles among producers, consumers, decomposers, air, water and soil and is conserved; energy flows in from the sun and out as heat and is not recycled. Students draw a system boundary around an ecosystem (a maple forest) and model where the atoms go and where the energy goes, including decomposers breaking down dead matter. Boundary: no chemical equations for the processes. Across bands it assumes s5-matter-movement (grade 5: the food web and matter cycle model; skips because grade 6 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit); s5-food-energy-sun (grade 5: energy in food came from the sun; skips because grade 6 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). food-web and matter-cycle rest in grade 6 (from s5-matter-movement): the base text has no grade 6 ecosystem unit. Load: development row (unit 7.4). Handoff kind: from s5-matter-movement (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s5-food-energy-sun (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Reactivation: food-web was last used in grade 5 and is not used in grade(s) 6, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the food-web model again before the new work.

words: population; resource; limiting factor; abundant; scarce; carrying capacity
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (population against time)
notes: Base unit 7.5 (rainforest cleared for palm oil and the animals that live there). Students analyze population data to show that when food, water, space or shelter is plentiful, organisms grow and populations rise, and when it is scarce they fall. The reasoning grows from one organism to a whole population over time. Across bands it assumes s5-matter-movement (grade 5: who eats whom in a food web; skips because grade 6 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). Load: development row (unit 7.5). Handoff kind: from s5-matter-movement (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: competition; predation; mutualism; parasitism; interaction; abiotic; biotic
notes: Base unit 7.5. The same kinds of interactions (competition, predator and prey, mutually beneficial partners) recur across very different ecosystems. Students use these patterns to predict what will happen to one population when another changes, in an ecosystem they have not studied. Builds on the grade 5 food web (s5-matter-movement) and on the grade 1 patterns of animal behaviour (s1-parent-offspring, 1.LS1.B in the articulation). Load: development row (unit 7.5). Handoff kind: from s5-matter-movement (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s1-parent-offspring (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s1-parent-offspring.

words: disruption; habitat loss; invasive species; biodiversity; argument
cross_subject: ela:W.7.1 (written argument with evidence)
notes: Base unit 7.5. Students argue from data that a change to the physical or living parts of an ecosystem (clearing, drought, a new species) changes its populations, and judge whether another group's evidence supports its claim. stability-change carries: it is the crosscutting concept of MS-LS2-4. Builds on s3-environment-change-solution (when an environment changes, some organisms survive and others do not; 3.LS2.C and 3.LS4.D in the articulation) and on the food web of s5-matter-movement, which students use to trace what a change does to other populations. Load: development row (unit 7.5). Handoff kind: from s3-environment-change-solution (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-environment-change-solution. Handoff kind: from s5-matter-movement (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: biodiversity; ecosystem service; trade-off; stakeholder; sustainable
cross_subject: ela:RI.7.8 (judge whether evidence supports a claim)
notes: Base unit 7.5. Students compare solutions that keep biodiversity and ecosystem services (clean water, soil, pollination) while meeting people's needs, such as farming methods and protected corridors, weighing scientific, economic and social constraints. Starts MS-ESS3-3 (human impacts; owned by s7-human-impact-design). Builds on s3-environment-change-solution (judging solutions when an environment changes) and s5-protect-resources (how communities protect resources); 3.LS4.D and 5.ESS3.C sit behind it. Load: development row (unit 7.5). Handoff kind: from s3-environment-change-solution (grade 3) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s4-energy-resources and s5-protect-resources. Handoff kind: from s5-protect-resources (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: criteria; constraints; precise; impact; stakeholder
notes: Base unit 7.5. Students define a design problem precisely enough to solve it: the need, measurable criteria for success, and constraints, including science limits and possible harm to people and the environment. Completes MS-ETS1-1, started in s6-hazard-forecast. Load: completion row (unit 7.5, finishing work begun in 6.5).

words: natural resource; mineral; ore; fossil fuel; groundwater; renewable; non-renewable; uneven distribution
notes: Base unit 7.6 (changing rain and water supply). Minerals, fossil fuels and groundwater are found where past and present geologic processes put them: oil where marine life was buried, metal ores near old volcanic zones, groundwater in porous rock, soil where rock weathers. Most are limited and non-renewable in a human lifetime, and people are using them up. Students explain a local or regional resource from the rock-cycle and plate models. Across bands it assumes s4-energy-resources (grade 4: energy and fuels come from natural resources; skips because grades 5 and 6 have no resource standard). Load: development row (unit 7.6). Handoff kind: from s4-energy-resources (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

model_in: water-cycle; energy-transfer; data-graph; cause-effect; stability-change; claim-evidence-reasoning
words: global temperature; greenhouse gas; carbon dioxide; methane; fossil fuel; climate change; correlation; cause
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.5 (summarize temperature records)
notes: Base unit 7.6. Students ask questions of temperature records, gas levels and human activity data to find what has raised the global temperature over the past century, separating correlation from cause, and link warmer air holding more water to the changing rain they started from. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5): human activities, chiefly burning fossil fuels, are the main cause; natural factors (sunlight, volcanoes) are weighed and found smaller. Load: development row (unit 7.6).

words: per capita; consumption; population growth; impact; rate
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent increase in population and use)
notes: Base unit 7.6. Students argue from data that as human population and use per person of water, food, minerals and energy rise, the effects on Earth systems grow unless technologies and choices change. Science describes the consequences; it does not decide what a society should do. Builds on s3-environment-change-solution and s5-protect-resources (3.LS2.C, 3.LS4.D and 5.ESS3.C in the articulation). Hands on to bio-biodiversity-simulation, where population and per-person use become parameters of a sustainability simulation (HS-ESS3-3). Load: development row (unit 7.6). Handoff kind: from s3-environment-change-solution (grade 3) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s4-energy-resources and s5-protect-resources. Handoff kind: from s5-protect-resources (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: monitor; minimize; human impact; water use; land use; pollution; solution
cross_subject: ela:W.7.7 (short research project)
notes: Base unit 7.6. Completes MS-ESS3-3, started in s7-biodiversity-solutions. Students design a method to monitor and reduce one human impact on water in their community (rain gardens, permeable paving, water reuse) and evaluate it against criteria and constraints. Teacher note: community water problems can touch families directly; keep the focus on solutions and on data, not blame. Across bands it assumes s5-protect-resources (grade 5: ways communities protect Earth resources; skips because grade 6 (base text order) has no human-impact unit). Load: completion row (unit 7.6, finishing work begun in 7.5). Handoff kind: from s5-protect-resources (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: force; collision; interaction; Newton's third law; equal; opposite; direction
cross_subject: math:7.NS.A.1 (opposite directions as positive and negative)
notes: Base unit 8.1 (a dropped phone that cracks or does not). In a collision, each object pushes on the other with a force of the same size in the opposite direction. Students draw force diagrams for collisions and apply this to design packaging or a case that protects an object. Taught in the same unit as MS-PS2-2 and MS-PS3-1, which 8.1 develops in full (s8-forces-motion-mass, s8-kinetic-energy-graphs), and starts MS-LS1-8 (touch and pressure receptors; owned by s8-senses-brain). Boundary: one dimension, vertical or horizontal. Teacher note: drop tests from low heights onto soft surfaces, eggs or phones replaced by safe stand-ins; eye protection when anything may break. Across bands it assumes s4-collisions (grade 4: objects collide and energy changes; skips because grades 5 to 7: grade 5 forces are gravity only and the base text puts collisions in unit 8.1). force-diagram rests in grades 6 and 7 (from grade 5, s5-gravity-down): the base text has no forces unit before 8.1. Load: development row (unit 8.1). Grade 8 holds 26 rows against 14 in grade 6 and 18 in grade 7 because the base text completes many expectations here after partial work in grades 6 and 7, and several grade 8 rows are short (marked in their Load line); the base text's unit lengths are balanced across the three years. Rows are expectation owners, not equal spans of time: the course frame plans days, not rows. Handoff kind: from s4-collisions (grade 4) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s4-collisions. Reactivation: force-diagram was last used in grade 5 and is not used in grade(s) 6, 7, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the force-diagram model again before the new work.

words: decision matrix; systematic; evaluate; weigh; criteria; constraints
cross_subject: math:6.EE.A.2c (weighted scores as an evaluated expression)
notes: Base unit 8.1. Students compare competing designs with a systematic process, such as a decision matrix that scores each design on each criterion and constraint, and choose the strongest. Completes MS-ETS1-2, started in s6-hazard-forecast and used in 7.2 and 7.6. Load: completion row (unit 8.1, finishing work begun in 6.5 and used in 7.2 and 7.6).

words: test data; compare; combine; redesign; best features
cross_subject: math:7.SP.B.4 (compare two data sets by center and spread)
notes: Base unit 8.1. Students analyze test results from several designs, find which features did best, and combine them into a new design that better meets the criteria. Completes MS-ETS1-3, used first in s7-design-optimize. Load: completion row (unit 8.1, used first in 7.2).

words: wave; vibration; amplitude; wavelength; frequency; pitch; medium; energy
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (describe a relationship from its graph)
notes: Base unit 8.2 (music from a truck shakes windows across a parking lot). Sound is a vibration passed through a medium by particles bumping their neighbours; it cannot cross empty space. A repeating wave is described by amplitude, wavelength and frequency; a larger amplitude carries more energy, which is why louder sound can shake a window. Students use graphs and simple numbers to relate amplitude and energy. Sound is also reflected, absorbed or transmitted by materials, the mechanical-wave half of MS-PS4-2 (owned by s6-light-paths, whose light model is reused). The wave-model, last used for signals in grade 6, is unused in grade 7 because the base text has no waves unit there. Boundary: no electromagnetic waves; standard repeating waves only. Teacher note: keep sound levels safe for hearing; no speakers held against ears. Assumes s6-light-paths across grade 7 (reflect, absorb, transmit now applied to sound); the base text has no waves unit in grade 7. Across bands it assumes s4-wave-model (grade 4: amplitude and wavelength of waves; skips because grades 5 to 7 have no waves standard in this order (base text unit 8.2)). Load: development row (unit 8.2). Handoff kind: from s6-light-paths (grade 6) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s4-wave-model (grade 4) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s4-wave-model. Reactivation: light-ray was last used in grade 6 and is not used in grade(s) 7, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the light-ray model again before the new work. Reactivation: wave-model was last used in grade 6 and is not used in grade(s) 7, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the wave-model model again before the new work.

words: stimulus; receptor; signal; nerve; brain; response; memory; senses
cross_subject: ela:W.8.8 (gather and combine information from several sources)
notes: Base unit 8.2. Completes MS-LS1-8, built from 6.1 (light receptors), 6.6 (nerves carry signals), 7.1 (smell), 8.1 (touch, pressure, heat) and here (hearing). Students gather and combine information showing that each kind of receptor responds to its own input and sends signals to the brain, which turns them into an immediate action or a memory. Boundary: not how the signal travels along a nerve. Load: completion row, short new work (hearing, unit 8.2; built in 6.1, 6.6, 7.1 and 8.1).

words: balanced; unbalanced; net force; mass; motion; reference frame; newton
cross_subject: math:7.NS.A.1 (net force as a sum of signed numbers)
notes: Base unit 8.1, where MS-PS2-2 is developed in full (the 8.1 unit page lists it without the partial mark): the force, mass and motion investigations come before the sound unit that uses them. Unit 8.3 (how a speaker moves without being touched) reuses it with non-contact forces (partial mark there). Students plan investigations, changing one variable at a time, showing that an object's change in motion depends on the total of the forces on it and its mass: balanced forces leave motion unchanged, unbalanced forces change it, and the same force changes a smaller mass more. Forces are given in newtons and from a stated frame of reference. Boundary: one dimension; no trigonometry. Across bands it assumes s3-balanced-forces (grade 3: balanced and unbalanced forces change motion (force arrows); skips because grades 4 to 7 have no contact-forces standard in this order (the base text puts forces in unit 8.1)). Stability and change, the crosscutting concept of MS-PS2-2: students explain why motion stays the same under balanced forces and changes under unbalanced ones. Load: development row (unit 8.1), applied in 8.3. Handoff kind: from s3-balanced-forces (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-balanced-forces.

words: kinetic energy; speed; mass; relationship; graph; non-linear
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (qualitative features of a graph); math:7.RP.A.2 (kinetic energy proportional to mass at a fixed speed)
notes: Base unit 8.1, where MS-PS3-1 is developed in full, including the quantitative mass and speed relationships, before unit 8.2; unit 8.3 applies it (partial mark there). Students build and read graphs showing that kinetic energy rises with mass and rises faster with speed (doubling speed far more than doubles the damage), keeping the two relationships separate. Carries the particle kinetic energy of grade 6 up to whole objects. Assumes s6-particle-temperature across grade 7: kinetic energy was met at the particle scale in grade 6, and grade 7 uses temperature but not the kinetic energy of whole objects. Across bands it assumes s4-speed-energy (grade 4: faster objects have more energy; skips because grades 5 to 7 have no motion-energy standard in this order). Math: the mass relationship is tested as a proportional relationship in a table (7.RP.A.2); the speed relationship is read as a non-linear graph (8.F.B.5). Load: development row (unit 8.1), applied in 8.3. Handoff kind: from s6-particle-temperature (grade 6) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s4-speed-energy (grade 4) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s4-speed-energy.

words: energy transfer; kinetic energy; evidence; inventory; before and after
cross_subject: ela:W.8.1 (written argument)
notes: Base unit 8.3 (partial mark there), applying MS-PS3-5, which grade 6 develops in full in 6.2 (s6-particle-temperature); the new work is whole objects rather than particles. Applies MS-PS3-5 (marked ~); s6-particle-temperature owns it. Students argue from evidence that whenever an object's kinetic energy changes (a cart slowing, a speaker cone moving, water warming), energy has been transferred to or from it, using a before and after energy inventory. Boundary: no energy calculations. Also hands on to chem-energy-accounting, which turns the before and after energy inventory into a computational model. Load: application row (unit 8.3; developed in 6.2). Handoff kind: from s6-particle-temperature (grade 6) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s7-reaction-energy.

words: magnet; electromagnet; coil; current; electric force; magnetic force; strength
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.2 (is force proportional to the number of turns)
notes: Base unit 8.3. Students ask questions about data to find what makes electric and magnetic forces stronger: more coil turns or more current in an electromagnet, stronger or closer magnets, more charge. They use this to explain how a speaker's coil and magnet push the cone. Boundary: quantitative answers limited to proportional reasoning. Teacher note: strong magnets can pinch skin and harm devices; keep them away from pacemakers; coils from low-voltage batteries only, disconnected when warm. Across bands it assumes s3-magnet-static (grade 3: electric and magnetic pulls without touching; skips because grades 4 to 7 have no electric or magnetic standard (base text unit 8.3)). Load: development row (unit 8.3). Handoff kind: from s3-magnet-static (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-magnet-static.

words: field; non-contact force; charge; magnetic field; evidence; experimental design
notes: Base unit 8.3. Students investigate magnets, charged tape and charged balloons, and judge their own experimental design, to give evidence that a field exists between objects that push or pull without touching. Boundary: electric and magnetic fields only; qualitative evidence. Across bands it assumes s3-magnet-static (grade 3: forces between objects not in contact; skips because grades 4 to 7 have no electric or magnetic standard (base text unit 8.3)). Introduces field-model (a field around a magnet or charge acts on another object at a distance), carried to grade 11 physics (phys-gravity-coulomb). Load: development row (unit 8.3). Handoff kind: from s3-magnet-static (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-magnet-static.

words: potential energy; stored energy; arrangement; distance; attract; repel
notes: Base unit 8.3. When two objects that interact at a distance are moved closer or farther apart, the energy stored in the system changes: lifting a book from the Earth, pulling magnets apart or bringing a charged balloon near hair. Students model the relative amounts. Boundary: two objects; electric, magnetic and gravitational; no calculation. Builds on pulls without touching (s3-magnet-static), gravity toward Earth's center (s5-gravity-down) and stored energy in a rubber-band or spring device (s4-energy-device); the standard has no articulation line, so these are judgment links. Load: development row (unit 8.3). Handoff kind: from s3-magnet-static (grade 3) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by s5-gravity-down. Handoff kind: from s5-gravity-down (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s4-energy-device (grade 4) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s4-energy-device.

words: orbit; rotation; axis; tilt; lunar phase; eclipse; season; reflect; wave model of light; brightness; color
notes: Base unit 8.4 (patterns in the sky). Students build a physical and drawn model of the Earth, sun and moon to explain the cycle of moon phases (sunlight reflected from the half of the moon facing the sun), solar and lunar eclipses (shadows when the three line up), and seasons (the tilt of the Earth's axis, not distance from the sun). Reuses the grade 6 light-ray model and the earlier earth-sun-moon model; neither is used in grade 7 because the base text has no grade 7 unit on light or the sky. Completes MS-PS4-2 in substance (the code sits on s6-light-paths, see there): students develop, revise and use a qualitative wave model of light that explains brightness, color, how materials reflect, absorb or transmit different colors, and why colors bend by different amounts at a surface; because light crosses empty space, it cannot be a matter wave like sound (8.4 unit page and scope and sequence DCI elements). The wave-model comes from s8-wave-amplitude-energy (8.2, taught earlier in the year) and is extended here from sound to light. Teacher note: never look at the sun directly or through a lens; eclipse viewing only through certified viewers or a pinhole projector. Assumes s6-light-paths across grade 7 because the base text places no light unit in grade 7. Across bands it assumes s5-shadows-sky (grade 5: patterns of shadows, day length and the seasonal sky; skips because grades 6 and 7 have no sky unit (base text unit 8.4)). Load: development row (unit 8.4), also finishing MS-PS4-2. Handoff kind: from s6-light-paths (grade 6) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s5-shadows-sky (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Reactivation: earth-sun-moon was last used in grade 6 and is not used in grade(s) 7, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the earth-sun-moon model again before the new work. Also owns MS-PS4-2: unit 8.4 completes the light model (the wave model of light explains brightness and colour) begun as rays in s6-light-paths.

words: gravity; gravitational force; mass; attract; distance; orbit
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.2 (tables of mass and force: does the pull grow in proportion to the mass); math:8.SP.A.1 (scatter plot of orbital period against distance)
notes: Base unit 8.4. Students argue from data (simulations, tables of mass, distance and orbital period) that gravity always attracts and is stronger between larger masses. Boundary: no law of gravitation formula; no Kepler's laws. Across bands it assumes s5-gravity-down (grade 5: gravity pulls objects toward Earth's center; skips because grades 6 and 7 have no gravity unit (base text unit 8.4)). Load: development row (unit 8.4). Handoff kind: from s5-gravity-down (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: solar system; galaxy; Milky Way; orbit; gravity; star
notes: Base unit 8.4. Gravity holds the solar system and the Milky Way together and controls the orbits within them. Students model orbits (physical or computer) and explain why planets keep circling instead of flying off or falling in. Boundary: no Kepler's laws. Across bands it assumes s5-gravity-down (grade 5: gravity as a pull toward the center of a body; skips because grades 6 and 7 have no gravity unit (base text unit 8.4)). Load: development row (unit 8.4). Handoff kind: from s5-gravity-down (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: scale; diameter; distance; astronomical unit; scale model; layer
cross_subject: math:8.EE.A.3 (powers of ten for very large numbers); math:7.G.A.1 (scale drawings)
notes: Base unit 8.4. Students analyze data on the sizes, distances and layers of objects in the solar system and build scale models showing how small the planets are against the distances between them. Boundary: no recall of facts about each planet. Across bands it assumes s5-star-brightness (grade 5: star distances and the scale of space; skips because grades 6 and 7 have no space unit (base text unit 8.4)). Load: development row (unit 8.4). Handoff kind: from s5-star-brightness (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: gene; chromosome; protein; mutation; trait; allele; harmful; beneficial
notes: Base unit 8.5 (cattle with extra-large muscles). Genes on chromosomes carry the instructions for proteins; proteins build structures and do jobs that make traits. A change to a gene (a mutation) can change the protein and so the trait, with harmful, helpful or no effect on the organism. Builds on rearranging molecules in s7-cell-respiration-growth. Boundary: the chromosome and protein scale only; no DNA bases, no protein synthesis steps, no named kinds of mutation. The base text limits neutral effects to the idea, since evidence for them sits below this scale. Students develop and use a model connecting a changed gene on a chromosome to a possible protein change and then to harmful, beneficial or neutral effects on the organism's structure and function; the teacher does not supply the model as an explanation. Keep the model above specific molecular changes. Load: development row (unit 8.5).

words: inherit; offspring; asexual; sexual reproduction; genetic variation; Punnett square; dominant; recessive
cross_subject: math:7.SP.C.8b (a Punnett square as a sample space for a compound event)
notes: Base unit 8.5. In asexual reproduction offspring get identical genetic information from one parent; in sexual reproduction each parent gives one of each pair of chromosomes, so offspring vary. Students use Punnett squares, diagrams and simulations to predict the chances of a trait. Teacher note: use animal and plant examples; never ask students to trace their own family's traits, which can expose adoption, donor conception or other private family facts. Across bands it assumes s3-inherited-traits (grade 3: traits are inherited from parents with variation; skips because grades 4 to 7 have no heredity standard (base text unit 8.5)). Load: development row (unit 8.5). Handoff kind: from s3-inherited-traits (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-inherited-traits.

words: nucleus; chloroplast; mitochondria; cell membrane; cell wall; organelle; function
notes: Base unit 8.5. Completes MS-LS1-2, built in 6.6 (membrane and wall), 7.4 (chloroplasts and mitochondria) and here (the nucleus holds the chromosomes). Students model the cell as a whole system and the role of each named part in it. Boundary: structure and function details only for the cell wall and membrane; the other parts only in relation to the whole cell; no biochemistry. Load: completion row, short new work (the nucleus, unit 8.5; built in 6.6 and 7.4).

words: environment; genetic factor; growth; variable; drought; fertilizer
cross_subject: math:8.SP.A.1 (scatter plots of growth against a condition)
notes: Base unit 8.5, completing work begun in 7.3 (food and growth). Completes MS-LS1-5. Students explain from data how both genes and conditions (food, light, water, space) affect how large an organism grows: seed varieties in drought, fish in large and small ponds, cattle breeds. Boundary: no genetic mechanisms or biochemistry. Across bands it assumes s3-environment-traits (grade 3: the environment changes how traits develop; skips because grades 4 to 7 have no heredity standard (base text unit 8.5)). Hands on to bio-mitosis-differentiation (HS-LS1-4), which gives the cell-level reason an organism grows: cells divide and differentiate. Load: completion row (unit 8.5, finishing work begun in 7.3). Handoff kind: from s3-environment-traits (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-environment-traits.

words: artificial selection; selective breeding; genetic engineering; gene therapy; technology; society
cross_subject: ela:W.8.8 (gather information from reliable sources)
notes: Base unit 8.5. Students gather and combine information from reliable sources on how people choose the traits of plants and animals (selective breeding, genetic modification) and treat genetic illness (gene therapy), and on the effects on society. Teacher note: questions of food and medicine choices are discussed as evidence and trade-offs; no student is asked to judge their own family's choices. Same-grade ground: follows s8-genes-proteins-traits and s8-inheritance in unit 8.5; no earlier-grade skill is assumed, since the standard has no articulation line below grade 8. Hands on to bio-dna-chromosomes-traits (HS-LS3-1): questions about how breeding and gene technology work become the testable questions about DNA and chromosomes asked there. Load: development row, short (unit 8.5).

words: fossil record; extinction; diversity; rock layer; common ancestor; complexity
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-timeline-deep-time (deep-time timeline)
notes: Base unit 8.6 (a fossil of a giant ancient penguin). Students analyze fossils in rock layers for patterns: which life forms appear when, which go extinct, and how body structures change over time, assuming natural laws worked then as now. Builds on reading rock layers in s6-geologic-time. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5). Boundary: no names of individual species or geologic eras. Assumes s6-geologic-time across grade 7: the base text puts rock layers in 6.4 and the fossil record in 8.6, with no grade 7 unit between. Load: development row (unit 8.6). Handoff kind: from s6-geologic-time (grade 6) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: anatomy; similar structure; homologous; evolutionary relationship; ancestor
notes: Base unit 8.6. Students compare the gross anatomy of living and fossil organisms (flipper, wing and arm bones) to explain which are more closely related and share more recent common ancestors. Builds on s3-fossils (fossils show living things have changed; 3.LS4.A in the articulation). Load: development row, short (unit 8.6). Handoff kind: from s3-fossils (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-fossils.

words: embryo; development; similarity; relatedness
notes: Base unit 8.6. Students compare pictures of embryos of different animals at matched stages to find similarities not seen in the adults, as further evidence of relatedness. Boundary: gross appearance only. Same-grade ground: follows s8-fossil-record and s8-anatomical-relationships in unit 8.6; no earlier-grade skill is assumed, since the standard has no articulation line below grade 8. Load: development row, short (unit 8.6).

words: natural selection; variation; adaptation; survive; reproduce; environment; probability
cross_subject: math:7.SP.C.6 (probability from observed frequencies)
notes: Base unit 8.6. Individuals in a population vary; in a given environment some variations raise the chance of surviving and having offspring, so those traits become more common. Students explain this with probability statements and proportional reasoning. Taught as the evidence shows (BASELINE rule 5). Across bands it assumes s3-variation-advantage (grade 3: variation gives some individuals an advantage in survival; skips because grades 4 to 7 have no evolution standard (base text unit 8.6)). Load: development row (unit 8.6). Handoff kind: from s3-variation-advantage (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-variation-advantage.

words: trait frequency; proportion; generation; increase; decrease; population change
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent change over generations)
notes: Base unit 8.6. Students use tables, graphs and simple simulations to show how the share of a trait in a population rises or falls over generations under natural selection. Boundary: no Hardy-Weinberg calculations. Builds on s3-habitat-survival and s3-variation-advantage (some individuals survive better in a habitat; 3.LS4.C in the articulation). Load: development row (unit 8.6). Handoff kind: from s3-habitat-survival (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-habitat-survival. Handoff kind: from s3-variation-advantage (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-variation-advantage.

words: courtship; pollination; pollinator; nectar; seed dispersal; reproduction; behavior
cross_subject: ela:W.8.1 (written argument)
notes: Base units 8.5 (flowers and pollinators) and 8.6 (animal behaviors). Completes MS-LS1-4. Students argue from evidence how animal behaviors (nest building, herding, calls and displays) and plant structures (bright flowers, nectar, hard shells) raise the chance of successful reproduction, including animals that help plants reproduce. Teacher note: reproduction is treated through plants and animal behavior, at the level of the standard. Across bands it assumes s3-animal-groups (grade 3: animal behaviours that raise survival; skips because grades 4 to 7 have no animal behaviour standard). Load: completion row (units 8.5 and 8.6). Handoff kind: from s3-animal-groups (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of s3-animal-groups.

words: carrying capacity; limiting factor; population; density-dependent; density-independent; model run
cross_subject: math:S-ID.B.6 (fit a function to population data over time); math:N-Q.A.2 (define the quantities a population model tracks)
notes: Explain why a population levels off, crashes or grows by using graphs and a simple computational model (a spreadsheet or a provided simulation) of births, deaths and resources. Factors compared: space and boundaries, food and water, climate, competition, predation; at more than one scale (a pond, a park, a region). The grade 7 food web and population ideas become quantitative: students change one input and predict the curve before running it. Introduces computational-model (a model that steps quantities forward by rules), used again in chemistry and physics. Limit (assessment boundary): students do not derive the equations; they use and adjust given ones. Across bands it assumes s7-resources-populations (grade 7: populations limited by resources; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). food-web rests in grade 8 (from grade 7): the base text has no grade 8 ecosystem unit. Biology holds 24 rows owning 30 expectations (all of life science, four engineering and three Earth and space, as Appendix K's modified domains map does), against 20 in Chemistry and 20 in Physics; several rows are short (bio-group-behavior) and five combine expectations, each with a Load line naming the distinct performances. The course frame plans days from those performances, not from row counts. Math readiness: the high school math named here (S-ID.B.6, N-Q.A.2) is not yet placed in a Curio Class math course, so this row supplies the scaffold (a provided function, table or spreadsheet step) until the math progression says when it is taught. Handoff kind: from s7-resources-populations (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Reactivation: food-web was last used in grade 7 and is not used in grade(s) 8, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the food-web model again before the new work.

words: biodiversity; species richness; abundance; sample; mean; trend
cross_subject: math:S-ID.A.2 (compare centre and spread of two data sets)
notes: Use averages, trends and side-by-side graphs of provided survey data (quadrat counts, bird counts, fishery records) to support and then revise an explanation of what changed biodiversity or a population in an ecosystem. The growth from middle school is revision: a second data set arrives and the class changes its explanation. Limit: provided data only (assessment boundary); no diversity index formulas required. Across bands it assumes s7-ecosystem-disruption (grade 7: changes to an ecosystem change its populations; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). Compare provided data at two clearly different ecosystem scales (for example a set of quadrats and a whole watershed), then revise the explanation when a second data set changes or limits the first conclusion. Math readiness: the high school math named here (S-ID.A.2) is not yet placed in a Curio Class math course, so this row supplies the scaffold (a provided function, table or spreadsheet step) until the math progression says when it is taught. Handoff kind: from s7-ecosystem-disruption (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: stability; disturbance; resilience; succession; equilibrium; new ecosystem
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (evaluate the argument and evidence in a text)
notes: Evaluate claims, evidence and reasoning that an ecosystem keeps similar numbers and kinds of organisms while conditions are stable, and that a large change (sea level rise, a volcanic eruption) can produce a different ecosystem, while a modest one (a seasonal flood, moderate hunting) is absorbed. Crosscutting concept: stability and change. Students judge whether an argument's evidence covers the scale of change it claims. Across bands it assumes s7-ecosystem-disruption (grade 7: arguing from data that ecosystem change shifts populations; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). stability-change carries from grade 7 (s7-ecosystem-disruption, s7-climate-change-evidence) and grade 8 (s8-forces-motion-mass, where MS-PS2-2 uses it). Handoff kind: from s7-ecosystem-disruption (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: group behaviour; flocking; schooling; cooperation; survival; reproduction
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (judge whether the evidence is relevant and sufficient)
notes: Evaluate evidence that group behaviour (flocking, schooling, herding, cooperative hunting, social insect colonies) changes an individual's and a species' chances to survive and reproduce. Students weigh study designs: what was measured, compared with what, and whether the evidence separates the group effect from other causes. Short skill, usually one section inside the ecosystems unit. Across bands it assumes s8-reproduction-behaviors (grade 8: behaviours that raise survival and reproduction).

words: criteria; constraint; trade-off; invasive species; habitat loss; mitigation
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.1 (units in quantitative criteria such as hectares or cost per year)
notes: Engineering first done in full here (HS-ETS1-1 is owned by this row and used again in chemistry and physics). Students analyse a large human impact on biodiversity (urban growth, a dam, an invasive species), state qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints that account for what people need and want, then design, evaluate and refine a solution that reduces the impact (HS-LS2-7). The grade 8 design cycle grows by adding numbers to criteria and by naming whose needs a constraint protects. Across bands it assumes s8-design-evaluate (grade 8: criteria and constraints for a design problem); s7-biodiversity-solutions (grade 7: designs that protect biodiversity; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). Frame the work as a major global biodiversity challenge (HS-ETS1-1). Use a local dam, urban expansion or invasive species case to investigate it, and connect the qualitative and quantitative criteria to societal needs and wants. Load: two performances: defining the global challenge with criteria and constraints (HS-ETS1-1), then designing, evaluating and refining a solution (HS-LS2-7). Math readiness: the high school math named here (N-Q.A.1) is not yet placed in a Curio Class math course, so this row supplies the scaffold (a provided function, table or spreadsheet step) until the math progression says when it is taught. Handoff kind: from s7-biodiversity-solutions (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: technological solution; prioritise; trade-off; reliability; impact data; pollutant
cross_subject: math:N-Q.A.3 (judge the precision of impact data used to compare solutions)
notes: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces human impact on natural systems (HS-ESS3-4, core idea ESS3.C, placed in Biology as NGSS Appendix K places it) using impact data (pollutant amounts, biomass and species diversity, land use change), and judge it against prioritised criteria and trade-offs: cost, safety, reliability, looks, and social, cultural and environmental effects (HS-ETS1-3, first done in full here, used again in chemistry and physics). Range from local (reuse and recycling) to large scale (geoengineering proposals), weighed on evidence, not on opinion. Across bands it assumes s8-design-test-combine (grade 8: testing and combining designs against criteria); s7-human-impact-design (grade 7: designs that lessen human impact on the environment; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no human-impact unit). Load: two performances: evaluating a solution with impact data (HS-ESS3-4), and weighing it against prioritised criteria and trade-offs (HS-ETS1-3). Math readiness: the high school math named here (N-Q.A.3) is not yet placed in a Curio Class math course, so this row supplies the scaffold (a provided function, table or spreadsheet step) until the math progression says when it is taught. Handoff kind: from s7-human-impact-design (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: photosynthesis; glucose; chloroplast; chemical energy; light energy; reactant; product
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.A.1 (read the parts of a balanced equation as counts of molecules)
notes: Use a model (diagram, balanced equation, conceptual model) to show how photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and water and, with light energy, makes sugar and oxygen, so light energy becomes chemical energy stored in the products. Builds on grade 7 photosynthesis by tracking atoms and energy separately and accounting for both. Limit: no light reactions, Calvin cycle or other biochemical steps (assessment boundary). Across bands it assumes s7-photosynthesis (grade 7: plants make food from carbon dioxide and water using light; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no cell-energy unit); s7-reactions-atoms (grade 7: atoms are conserved as they rearrange in reactions; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no reactions unit). matter-cycle rests in grade 8 (from grade 7): the base text has no grade 8 unit on matter in living things. Math readiness: the high school math named here (A-SSE.A.1) is not yet placed in a Curio Class math course, so this row supplies the scaffold (a provided function, table or spreadsheet step) until the math progression says when it is taught. Handoff kind: from s7-photosynthesis (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s7-reactions-atoms (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Reactivation: matter-cycle was last used in grade 7 and is not used in grade(s) 8, where no standard calls for it; this row opens with a short task in which students draw or use the matter-cycle model again before the new work.

words: cellular respiration; aerobic; anaerobic; fermentation; bond; net energy transfer
notes: Model cellular respiration as a chemical process: bonds in food molecules and oxygen break, bonds in carbon dioxide and water form, and the difference is a net release of energy the cell uses (HS-LS1-7). Then explain, with evidence, how matter cycles and energy flows when oxygen is present and when it is not, in places such as waterlogged soil, muscle in hard exercise and bread dough (HS-LS2-3). Bond energy stays qualitative here; chemistry makes it a model of total bond energy. Limit: no steps of glycolysis or the Krebs cycle, no specific chemical processes (both assessment boundaries). Teacher note: yeast and dough investigations use warm water only, no flames. Across bands it assumes s7-cell-respiration-growth (grade 7: food molecules react with oxygen to release energy; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no cell-energy unit); s7-reaction-energy (grade 7: reactions release or absorb energy; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no reactions unit). After an initial explanation, provide contrasting aerobic and anaerobic evidence; students revise their explanation of matter cycling and energy flow and name the evidence that made them revise (HS-LS2-3 asks for construct and revise). Load: two performances that each need time: a model of respiration as bonds breaking and forming (HS-LS1-7), then an explanation of matter and energy with and without oxygen, revised on new evidence (HS-LS2-3). Handoff kind: from s7-cell-respiration-growth (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s7-reaction-energy (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: amino acid; protein; carbon-based molecule; sugar; element; large molecule
notes: Construct and revise an explanation, from models and simulations, of how the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in sugar from photosynthesis combine with other elements (such as nitrogen and sulfur) to build amino acids and other large carbon-based molecules. Links the matter story (where does a tree's mass come from) to growth. Limit: no details of the specific reactions and no identifying macromolecules by name as the goal (assessment boundary). Across bands it assumes s7-food-molecules (grade 7: large food molecules made of repeating subunits; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no molecules unit); s7-cell-respiration-growth (grade 7: atoms of food rearranged into molecules for growth; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no cell-energy unit). Handoff kind: from s7-food-molecules (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from s7-cell-respiration-growth (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: trophic level; biomass; energy pyramid; producer; consumer; conservation of matter
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent of stored energy passed from one trophic level to the next)
notes: Use a mathematical model of stored energy in biomass to show how energy passes from one trophic level to the next (roughly a tenth carried up, the rest released as heat by respiration), and that carbon, oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen atoms are conserved as matter cycles. Grows the grade 7 food web into proportional accounting. Limit: proportional reasoning only (assessment boundary). Across bands it assumes s7-ecosystem-matter-energy (grade 7: energy flow and matter cycling among organisms; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). Handoff kind: from s7-ecosystem-matter-energy (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: carbon cycle; biosphere; atmosphere; hydrosphere; geosphere; reservoir; flux
notes: Develop a model of how photosynthesis and cellular respiration move carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and geosphere (models may be diagrams, simulations or simple mathematical models). Students mark which arrows are biological and which are not, and where carbon is stored for a long time. Hands the matter-cycle model to chemistry, which makes the whole carbon cycle quantitative (HS-ESS2-6). Limit: no chemical steps of photosynthesis or respiration (assessment boundary). Across bands it assumes s7-ecosystem-matter-energy (grade 7: matter cycles between living and non-living parts; skips because grade 8 (base text order) has no ecosystem unit). Handoff kind: from s7-ecosystem-matter-energy (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: cell; tissue; organ; organ system; hierarchy; interacting systems
notes: Develop and use a model of the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism (cells, tissues, organs, organ systems) and how systems interact to do whole-organism jobs: taking in nutrients, delivering water, moving in response to a nerve signal. Example: an artery depends on elastic tissue and smooth muscle to deliver the right amount of blood. Grows the grade 6 cell and body systems unit into interacting levels. Limit: nothing at the molecular or chemical reaction level (assessment boundary). Across bands it assumes s7-body-systems-food (grade 7: cells form tissues, organs and body systems that work together; skips because grade 8 builds on it only for the senses). Handoff kind: from s7-body-systems-food (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: homeostasis; feedback; negative feedback; set point; stimulus; response
cross_subject: math:S-ID.A.1 (plot and compare repeated measurements)
notes: Plan and conduct an investigation that gives evidence of feedback keeping a condition steady: heart rate and recovery after exercise, stomata opening with moisture and temperature, root growth toward water. Students choose what to vary and hold steady and read the data for a return toward a set point. Limit: not the cellular processes inside the feedback (assessment boundary).
